result.overall: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding that the trial judge's verdict convicting Sergeant Beaudry of obstructing justice was not unreasonable, as it was supported by a plausible interpretation of the evidence and proper assessment of credibility.

themes.name: Police discretion
themes.summary: Police discretion is essential but must be exercised honestly, transparently, and on valid grounds; improper exercise does not automatically constitute obstructing justice.

themes.name: Reasonableness of verdict
themes.summary: The appellate court must determine if the trial judge's verdict was one a reasonable jury could have rendered, giving deference to credibility assessments and considering all evidence.

themes.name: Credibility and evidence assessment
themes.summary: The verdict depended heavily on the trial judge's assessment of the accused's credibility and the plausibility of explanations offered for not taking breath samples.

themes.name: Relationship between obstructing justice and police discretion
themes.summary: The offence requires specific intent to obstruct justice; improper discretion alone is insufficient for conviction.

themes.name: Legal context and administrative directives
themes.summary: Administrative directives and Crown prosecutor discretion do not limit police discretion, which is grounded in common law and statute.

arguments.quote: In answer to the charge, Mr. Beaudry contended that his decision was a proper exercise of police discretion.
arguments.claim: Mr. Beaudry contended that his decision not to gather evidence was a proper exercise of police discretion.

arguments.quote: The Crown argued that the decision was founded not on police discretion, but on preferential treatment of a fellow police officer.
arguments.claim: The Crown argued that Mr. Beaudry's decision was not an exercise of police discretion but preferential treatment of a fellow police officer.

arguments.quote: Mr. Beaudry was tried by a judge sitting alone and was convicted. The decision of Judge Beaulieu of the Court of Québec was upheld by the Quebec Court of Appeal, Chamberland J.A. dissenting: [2005] R.J.Q. 2536, 2005 QCCA 966.
arguments.claim: Mr. Beaudry was convicted by Judge Beaulieu of the Court of Québec, and this conviction was upheld by the Quebec Court of Appeal, with Chamberland J.A. dissenting.

arguments.quote: Chamberland J.A. considered it unreasonable to [translation] “reject the appellant’s explanations, or at least to find that they did not raise a reasonable doubt as to whether he had honestly exercised his discretion as a police officer not to involve the courts in the case” (para. 65).
arguments.claim: Chamberland J.A. dissented, finding it unreasonable to reject Mr. Beaudry's explanations or to find that they did not raise a reasonable doubt about whether he honestly exercised his discretion not to involve the courts.

arguments.quote: This discretion makes it possible to apply the law more fairly in real‑life situations faced by the police.
arguments.claim: Police discretion allows the law to be applied more fairly in real-life situations faced by police.

arguments.quote: On this subject, I cannot agree completely with the reasons of the majority of the Court of Appeal, which were written by Doyon J.A. Rather, I agree with the legal analysis of Chamberland J.A., in dissent. With respect, I believe that Doyon J.A. has unduly limited the scope of the discretionary power by considering extrinsic factors such as internal directives, which do not have the force of law, and the discretion of Crown prosecutors.
arguments.claim: The majority of the Court of Appeal unduly limited the scope of police discretionary power by considering extrinsic factors such as internal directives and Crown prosecutors' discretion, which do not have the force of law.

arguments.quote: 4 As I will explain, the verdict of the Court of Québec judge is reasonable and it is supported by a perfectly plausible interpretation of the evidence.
arguments.claim: The verdict of the Court of Québec judge is reasonable and supported by a plausible interpretation of the evidence.

arguments.quote: With respect, I believe that Chamberland J.A.’s analysis of the evidence is incompatible with the role of an appellate court in reviewing whether a verdict is unreasonable.
arguments.claim: Chamberland J.A.'s analysis of the evidence is incompatible with the role of an appellate court in reviewing whether a verdict is unreasonable.

arguments.quote: In the instant case, the trial judge made no error of law.
arguments.claim: The trial judge made no error of law in this case.

arguments.quote: It is apparent from the record that there was evidence to support each element of the offence.
arguments.claim: There was evidence to support each element of the offence.

arguments.quote: The resolution of the determinative issue turned on the credibility of the accused.
arguments.claim: The determinative issue turned on the credibility of the accused.

arguments.quote: The trial judge was in the best position to assess the credibility of the witnesses and to determine whether the evidence left room for a reasonable doubt.
arguments.claim: The trial judge was best positioned to assess witness credibility and determine if there was reasonable doubt.

arguments.quote: Assistant Director Rocheleau did not accept this explanation and ordered Sergeant Beaudry to prepare an impaired driving report. In response to pressure from the assistant director, an occurrence report entitled [translation] “Impaired Driving” was filed. As the report was only a few lines long, the senior officers of the Repentigny police were not satisfied with it, and they required that a proper report be written. A detailed report was not submitted until later that night.
arguments.claim: Assistant Director Rocheleau did not accept Sergeant Beaudry's explanation and ordered an impaired driving report to be prepared, which was initially minimal and later detailed.

arguments.quote: 13 After setting out the evidence introduced by the parties in great detail, Judge Beaulieu reviewed the applicable law. He began by discussing the burden of proof, and correctly pointed out that the Crown had the onus of proving the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt. Because the accused had testified at trial, and because it was necessary to assess the credibility of his testimony, Judge Beaulieu instructed himself in accordance with the principles set out by this Court in R. v. W. (D.), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu reviewed the law including burden of proof and the need to assess credibility of the accused's testimony per R. v. W. (D.).

arguments.quote: He observed that to find the accused guilty requires more than just disbelief of his version of the facts. It must also be determined whether that version raises a reasonable doubt, or whether it is possible, based on the evidence as a whole, to find beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty.
arguments.claim: To find the accused guilty requires more than disbelief of his version; it must be shown beyond reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty.

arguments.quote: 14 Judge Beaulieu then considered the offence of obstructing justice and noted that the Crown had to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused had the specific intent to obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice when he chose not to have Patrick Plourde take a breathalyzer test even though he had reasonable grounds to believe that Mr. Plourde had been driving while impaired.
arguments.claim: The Crown must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had specific intent to obstruct justice by not having Mr. Plourde take a breathalyzer test despite reasonable grounds to believe he was impaired.

arguments.quote: Judge Beaulieu added that more than a breach of ethics, inappropriate or unprofessional conduct, or an error in judgment was needed for the accused to be found guilty.
arguments.claim: More than a breach of ethics or error in judgment is needed to find the accused guilty of obstructing justice.

arguments.quote: 15 The main argument advanced by the defence was that Sergeant Beaudry’s decision not to gather the evidence needed to lay criminal charges against Patrick Plourde was, as he had explained to Assistant Director Rocheleau at the first interview, a proper exercise of his discretionary power.
arguments.claim: Sergeant Beaudry's decision not to gather evidence to lay charges was a proper exercise of his discretionary power.

arguments.quote: He observed that no directions can be found in the Criminal Code concerning the exercise of police discretion. Nonetheless, he noted that law enforcement and the proper functioning of the criminal justice system require that it be exercised on a daily basis.
arguments.claim: No directions exist in the Criminal Code about police discretion, but it must be exercised daily for law enforcement and justice system functioning.

arguments.quote: He therefore concluded that the outcome of the trial turned entirely on whether the court was satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Alain Beaudry had decided not to have Mr. Plourde take a breathalyzer test because Mr. Plourde was a Sûreté du Québec officer. In short, if Sergeant Beaudry was lenient because Mr. Plourde was a peace officer, the exercise of his discretion was unacceptable.
arguments.claim: The trial outcome depended on whether Sergeant Beaudry decided not to have Mr. Plourde take a breathalyzer test because he was a Sûreté du Québec officer; leniency for that reason is unacceptable.

arguments.quote: 17 Then, in reviewing the evidence, Judge Beaulieu did not call into question the description given by the accused and his colleagues of Mr. Plourde’s behaviour during the police intervention. However, he was of the opinion that the justifications offered by the three police officers who were at the scene were lies and were designed to explain, after the fact, the decision not to pursue the investigation.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu did not question the description of Mr. Plourde's behaviour but found the justifications by the police officers to be lies designed to explain the decision not to investigate further.

arguments.quote: As for Constable Boucher, Judge Beaulieu characterized as a lie his statement that he had not taken the initiative to have Mr. Plourde take a breathalyzer test because he had only a suspicion of impaired driving. Constable Boucher’s testimony was inconsistent with his incident report, in which he had stated that [translation] “[w]e quickly observed that the individual was in an advanced state of intoxication.”
arguments.claim: Constable Boucher's testimony that he only suspected impaired driving was a lie inconsistent with his incident report stating Mr. Plourde was clearly intoxicated.

arguments.quote: Judge Beaulieu also rejected the explanation given by Constable Bélisle. Even though Constable Bélisle had signed the report prepared by Constable Boucher, he testified that it had been difficult for him to determine that night whether the case was one of impaired driving, whereas it had seemed obvious to him that Mr. Plourde was in a crisis situation.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu rejected Constable Bélisle's explanation that it was difficult to determine impaired driving, noting he found Mr. Plourde was in crisis.

arguments.quote: 18 Judge Beaulieu also rejected the justification offered by the accused, Alain Beaudry, characterizing it as [translation] “an argument thought of after the fact to try to explain why he acted as he did on September 22”. In the judge’s opinion, it was not until his actions were questioned that Sergeant Beaudry invoked Mr. Plourde’s health to justify his decision.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu rejected Sergeant Beaudry's justification as an after-the-fact argument to explain his actions when questioned.

arguments.quote: 19 Judge Beaulieu first observed that Sergeant Beaudry had tried to conceal the true nature of the intervention by originally describing it as assistance to the public and then opting to call it an “unclassified activity” even though he knew that it was an impaired driving case.
arguments.claim: Sergeant Beaudry tried to conceal the true nature of the intervention by initially describing it as assistance to the public and then as an unclassified activity, despite knowing it was an impaired driving case.

arguments.quote: In his opinion, if Mr. Plourde was so depressed that it was inappropriate either to arrest him or to detain him in a cell for fear that he would do something unfortunate, the accused should have disregarded his refusal and taken him to the hospital.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu found that if Mr. Plourde was too depressed to arrest or detain safely, Sergeant Beaudry should have taken him to hospital instead of respecting his refusal to take a breathalyzer test.

arguments.quote: Likewise, Judge Beaulieu found no explanation for the failure to mention this consideration in the documents prepared that night — namely the occurrence report countersigned by the accused and his own activity log — even though Sergeant Beaudry had said at trial that it was what had convinced him to make his decision.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu found no explanation for failure to mention Mr. Plourde's depressive state in official documents despite Sergeant Beaudry's trial claim that it influenced his decision.

arguments.quote: In Judge Beaulieu’s opinion, Sergeant Beaudry’s explanation, that he had been thinking of the case of a police officer who had committed suicide at home after undergoing a breathalyzer test, did not make sense, because Mr. Plourde was safe in a room under camera surveillance.
arguments.claim: Sergeant Beaudry's explanation that he was thinking of a past police officer suicide case did not make sense because Mr. Plourde was under camera surveillance and safe.

arguments.quote: 21 Judge Beaulieu also questioned Sergeant Beaudry’s statement that he had had the interview of September 12 in mind that night.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu questioned Sergeant Beaudry's statement that he had the interview of September 12 in mind that night.

arguments.quote: According to Sergeant Beaudry, the woman had advised Mr. Plourde to go back to see his doctor because he was in a state of depression.
arguments.claim: According to Sergeant Beaudry, the woman had advised Mr. Plourde to go back to see his doctor because he was in a state of depression.

arguments.quote: The judge noted that Mr. Plourde himself did not remember that his sick leave had been mentioned.
arguments.claim: The judge noted that Mr. Plourde himself did not remember that his sick leave had been mentioned.

arguments.quote: Furthermore, the occurrence report written after that interview and countersigned by the accused made no mention of a depressive state.
arguments.claim: The occurrence report written after that interview and countersigned by the accused made no mention of a depressive state.

arguments.quote: Rather, it said that the woman was complaining about being harassed and that she believed Mr. Plourde to be mentally disturbed.
arguments.claim: The occurrence report said that the woman was complaining about being harassed and that she believed Mr. Plourde to be mentally disturbed.

arguments.quote: 22 Judge Beaulieu also accepted Constable Raymond Dagenais’s testimony that, when he had asked Sergeant Beaudry what Mr. Plourde was doing in the detention room for minors, Sergeant Beaudry had replied that Mr. Plourde was under arrest for impaired driving.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu accepted Constable Raymond Dagenais's testimony that Sergeant Beaudry said Mr. Plourde was under arrest for impaired driving when asked what he was doing in the detention room for minors.

arguments.quote: In addition, he believed Constable Dagenais’s statement that Sergeant Beaudry had told him to wait before photographing Mr. Plourde, because he had to make a decision about him.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu believed Constable Dagenais's statement that Sergeant Beaudry told him to wait before photographing Mr. Plourde because he had to make a decision about him.

arguments.quote: Again, Judge Beaulieu found these answers to be inconsistent with Sergeant Beaudry’s explanation.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu found these answers inconsistent with Sergeant Beaudry's explanation.

arguments.quote: Why would he have told Constable Dagenais that Mr. Plourde was under arrest if Mr. Plourde was in the room for minors for humanitarian reasons?
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu questioned why Sergeant Beaudry would say Mr. Plourde was under arrest if he was in the room for minors for humanitarian reasons.

arguments.quote: And why would he have told Constable Dagenais to wait before photographing Mr. Plourde if it had already been decided to characterize the case as an “unclassified activity”?
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu questioned why Sergeant Beaudry would tell Constable Dagenais to wait before photographing Mr. Plourde if it had already been decided to characterize the case as an 'unclassified activity'.

arguments.quote: In Judge Beaulieu’s view, the sole purpose of the occurrence report and the memorandum addressed to Assistant Director Rocheleau was to divert attention from the fact that Sergeant Beaudry had already decided at the scene of the traffic stop not to make the investigation that was called for under the circumstances.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu viewed the occurrence report and memorandum as attempts to divert attention from Sergeant Beaudry's decision not to conduct the investigation required under the circumstances.

arguments.quote: 23 This is what led the judge to conclude that on September 22, 2000, Alain Beaudry had deliberately failed to perform his duty, instead giving [translation] “a chance, preferential treatment, a privilege” to Patrick Plourde, a peace officer of the Sûreté du Québec.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu concluded that on September 22, 2000, Alain Beaudry deliberately failed to perform his duty, giving preferential treatment to Patrick Plourde, a peace officer of the Sûreté du Québec.

arguments.quote: Sergeant Beaudry could not have been unaware that breath samples were necessary items of evidence for laying a charge against Mr. Plourde under s. 253 of the Criminal Code .
arguments.claim: Sergeant Beaudry could not have been unaware that breath samples were necessary evidence for laying a charge against Mr. Plourde under s. 253 of the Criminal Code.

arguments.quote: The judge therefore found him guilty.
arguments.claim: The judge found Sergeant Beaudry guilty.

arguments.quote: 24 Chamberland J.A. began his analysis by noting that the trial judge had regarded the failure to gather evidence as the actus reus of the offence.
arguments.claim: The trial judge regarded the failure to gather evidence as the actus reus of the offence.

arguments.quote: In his opinion, however, this was the case only if Sergeant Beaudry had a legal obligation to gather that evidence. Since the officer had exercised his discretion, he did not have an obligation to gather evidence that could be used to lay criminal charges.
arguments.claim: Sergeant Beaudry had a legal obligation to gather evidence for the offence to be made out.

arguments.quote: 25 According to Chamberland J.A., police discretion exists in matters of criminal justice and is a response to, among other things, the community’s wish that not all those who commit minor offences should be arrested by the police or prosecuted. He added that the police may exercise this discretion in respect of anyone, including a fellow police officer, as long as they do so honestly, transparently, and on valid and reasonable grounds.
arguments.claim: Police discretion exists in criminal justice to avoid prosecuting minor offences and can be exercised honestly, transparently, and on valid and reasonable grounds, even regarding fellow officers.

arguments.quote: 26 Referring to Sergeant Beaudry’s testimony concerning the instruction he had received at the Institut de police and to the police practices manual (Guide de pratiques policières) of Repentigny’s public safety service, Chamberland J.A. concluded that Sergeant Beaudry was right to believe that he had the discretionary power to deal with Patrick Plourde’s case otherwise than through prosecution. In his view, whether Sergeant Beaudry had a duty to gather evidence depends, in short, on whether the discretion was exercised honestly.
arguments.claim: Sergeant Beaudry was right to believe he had discretionary power to deal with the case other than through prosecution, and whether he had a duty to gather evidence depends on whether discretion was exercised honestly.

arguments.quote: However, I feel that he exceeded the limits of his role in reinterpreting the evidence presented at trial and interfering with the assessment of the credibility of certain witnesses without showing appropriate deference to the trial judge’s findings. His analysis should have focussed on the question whether the trial judge’s verdict was reasonable.
arguments.claim: Chamberland J.A. exceeded his role by reinterpreting evidence and interfering with credibility assessments without deference to the trial judge, and should have focused on whether the verdict was reasonable.

arguments.quote: 28 Chamberland J.A. cited a number of facts in respect of which he disagreed with the trial judge’s interpretation: · Sergeant Beaudry explained that he was motivated to do what he did by Mr. Plourde’s depressive state. · That explanation was not contradicted either by the fact that Sergeant Beaudry decided at the scene of the traffic stop not to involve the criminal courts or by the use of the R‑400 code for “unclassified activity”. · Sergeant Beaudry did not at any time conceal anything. The occurrence report he countersigned stated that the individual was in an advanced state of intoxication and smelled strongly of alcohol. He also mentioned in his log book that the appellant was [translation] “sleeping it off”. · Sergeant Beaudry took Mr. Plourde to the police station and put him in a room equipped with a surveillance camera. · If Sergeant Beaudry had decided to help Mr. Plourde because he was a police officer, he could simply have driven him home. · The fact that the word “depression” does not appear anywhere in the accused’s report cannot be determinative in the instant case. The report also contains an objective description of what some would associate with depressed behaviour: crying fits, and the need to protect Mr. Plourde by putting him in the room reserved for young offenders. · Sergeant Beaudry suggested that his superior officer contact Mr. Plourde’s superior officer at the Sûreté du Québec, which is not indicative of an intent to cover the case up. · Although the trial judge saw Assistant Director Rocheleau’s testimony that Sergeant Beaudry had exercised his discretion [translation] “to give [Mr. Plourde] a chance” as an indication that the accused was lying about his intention, this comment by the accused was in fact neutral. · The record contains no evidence of falsification or alteration of documents or of an intention to mislead anyone regarding Mr. Plourde’s condition at the time of the events. Chamberland J.A. accordingly concluded that it was unreasonable to reject the appellant’s explanation, or at least to decide that the explanation did not raise a reasonable doubt as to whether he had decided honestly to exercise his discretion not to set the judicial process in motion.
arguments.claim: The trial judge's interpretation of facts such as Sergeant Beaudry's motivation, lack of concealment, and objective descriptions of the appellant's condition was incorrect and unreasonable to reject the appellant's explanation.
arguments.outcome_note: Court agrees with some factual points but finds Chamberland J.A. exceeded his role in reinterpreting evidence.

arguments.quote: The dissenting judge would therefore have substituted an acquittal for the guilty verdict. 3.2 Doyon J.A.
arguments.claim: Chamberland J.A. would have substituted an acquittal for the guilty verdict based on his analysis.
arguments.outcome_note: This is a dissenting opinion, not the Court's final holding.

arguments.quote: 29 Doyon J.A., writing for the majority of the Court of Appeal, did not dispute the existence of police discretion. However, it was his opinion that an assessment of the exercise of that discretion requires consideration of both the facts in issue and the legal context.
arguments.claim: Police discretion exists but its exercise requires consideration of both facts and legal context.

arguments.quote: 30 He began by stating that the circumstances giving rise to the police action led by Sergeant Beaudry were sufficiently serious that the trial judge had to be circumspect in considering the appellant’s version of the facts. As I will explain below, I agree with Doyon J.A. on this point.
arguments.claim: The seriousness of the circumstances required the trial judge to be circumspect in considering the appellant's version of facts.

arguments.quote: 31 Where we disagree, however, is on the weight to be attached in the analysis to the legal context.
arguments.claim: Disagreement with Doyon J.A. concerns the weight to be given to the legal context in analyzing police discretion.

arguments.quote: On this point, Doyon J.A. noted that in Quebec, criminal charges are generally authorized and laid by a Crown prosecutor. Sergeant Beaudry’s decision to exercise his discretion by not arresting Mr. Plourde and not requiring him to take a breathalyzer test must be assessed in that light.
arguments.claim: In Quebec, criminal charges are generally authorized and laid by a Crown prosecutor, so police discretion not to arrest or require breathalyzer must be assessed in that light.

arguments.quote: The consequence of the failure to take breath samples despite the existence of reasonable grounds to believe that an offence had been committed was to prevent the prosecutor from performing his or her functions. Doyon J.A. was accordingly of the opinion that, in determining whether a discretionary power has been properly exercised, the impact of the decision on the administration of justice, and in particular on the Attorney General’s ability to discharge his or her duties based on all the useful and relevant information, must not be overlooked.
arguments.claim: Failure to take breath samples despite reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed prevented the prosecutor from performing functions, impacting administration of justice and Attorney General's duties.

arguments.quote: 32 Further, still on the subject of the legal context, Doyon J.A. noted that the police practices manual of Repentigny’s public safety service contained, in addition to the passage quoted by Chamberland J.A., detailed instructions regarding the procedure to be followed in impaired driving cases, and that those instructions showed that the authorities clearly intended such offences to be investigated thoroughly from the outset.
arguments.claim: The police practices manual contained detailed instructions for impaired driving cases showing authorities intended thorough investigation from the outset.

arguments.quote: He therefore felt that it was open to the trial judge to find that Sergeant Beaudry had not exercised his discretion honestly.
arguments.claim: It was open to the trial judge to find that Sergeant Beaudry had not exercised his discretion honestly.

arguments.quote: 33 Doyon J.A. then rejected Chamberland J.A.’s interpretation of the evidence. Unlike the dissenting judge, however, Doyon J.A. came to the conclusion that there was no fatal error in the trial judgment.
arguments.claim: Doyon J.A. rejected Chamberland J.A.'s interpretation of the evidence but concluded there was no fatal error in the trial judgment.

arguments.quote: 35 There is no question that police officers have a duty to enforce the law and investigate crimes. The principle that the police have a duty to enforce the criminal law is well established at common law: R. v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner, [1968] 1 All E.R. 763 (C.A.), per Lord Denning, M.R., at p. 769; Hill v. Chief Constable of West Yorkshire, [1988] 2 All E.R. 238 (H.L.), per Lord Keith of Kinkel; P. Ceyssens, Legal Aspects of Policing (loose‑leaf ed.), vol. 1, at pp. 2‑22 et seq. 36 Moreover, this principle is codified in s. 48 of the Police Act, R.S.Q., c. P‑13.1: 48. The mission of police forces and of each police force member is to maintain peace, order and public security, to prevent and repress crime and, according to their respective jurisdiction as set out in sections 50 and 69, offences under the law and municipal by‑laws, and to apprehend offenders.
arguments.claim: Police officers have a duty to enforce the law and investigate crimes, a principle well established at common law and codified in s. 48 of the Police Act, R.S.Q., c. P‑13.1.

arguments.quote: 37 Nevertheless, it should not be concluded automatically, or without distinction, that this duty is applicable in every situation. Applying the letter of the law to the practical, real‑life situations faced by police officers in performing their everyday duties requires that certain adjustments be made. Although these adjustments may sometimes appear to deviate from the letter of the law, they are crucial and are part of the very essence of the proper administration of the criminal justice system, or to use the words of s. 139(2) , are perfectly consistent with the “course of justice”. The ability — indeed the duty — to use one’s judgment to adapt the process of law enforcement to individual circumstances and to the real‑life demands of justice is in fact the basis of police discretion.
arguments.claim: The police duty to enforce the law is not applicable in every situation; police discretion allows officers to adapt law enforcement to individual circumstances and real-life demands of justice.

arguments.quote: Thus, a police officer who has reasonable grounds to believe that an offence has been committed, or that a more thorough investigation might produce evidence that could form the basis of a criminal charge, may exercise his or her discretion to decide not to engage the judicial process. But this discretion is not absolute. Far from having carte blanche, police officers must justify their decisions rationally.
arguments.claim: Police officers may exercise discretion not to engage the judicial process if they have reasonable grounds to believe an offence has been committed or further investigation might produce evidence, but this discretion is not absolute and must be rationally justified.

arguments.quote: However, the officer’s sincere belief that he properly exercised his discretion is not sufficient to justify his decision.
arguments.claim: An officer's sincere belief in proper exercise of discretion is insufficient to justify the decision; objective justification is also required.

arguments.quote: However, I do not agree with him on the importance of the factors he regarded as part of the legal context, that is, the administrative directives and the administration of justice in the province. 4.1.1 Material Circumstances
arguments.claim: The administrative directives and administration of justice in the province are less important factors in assessing police discretion than material circumstances.

arguments.quote: In the first case, the interests of justice may very well be served if the officer gives the young offender a stern warning and alerts his or her parents.
arguments.claim: For minor offences like shoplifting by a teenager, police discretion may justify a stern warning and parental alert rather than arrest.

arguments.quote: However, this does not mean that the police have no discretion left when the degree of seriousness reaches a certain level. In the case of a robbery, or an even more serious offence, the discretion can be exercised to decide not to arrest a suspect or not to pursue an investigation. However, the justification offered must be proportionate to the seriousness of the conduct and it must be clear that the discretion was exercised in the public interest.
arguments.claim: For serious offences like robbery, police discretion may allow not arresting or pursuing investigation, but justification must be proportionate and in the public interest.

arguments.quote: Thus, while some exercises of discretion are almost routine and are clearly justified, others are truly exceptional and will require that the police officer explain his or her decision in greater detail.
arguments.claim: Routine exercises of police discretion are clearly justified, but exceptional cases require detailed explanation of the decision.

arguments.quote: 41 In the case at bar, it is clear from the evidence that, while the events that led to the police action did not represent the gravest of all possible situations, they were nonetheless serious. The officers originally intervened because Mr. Plourde was driving at high speed with a flat tire. He also drove through a stop sign, almost hit the median, and continued to drive for some distance even though the patrol car’s lights were flashing. Once Sergeant Beaudry suspected that the individual had been drinking, he had to be even more circumspect in deciding how to act.
arguments.claim: The events leading to the police action were serious, involving high-speed driving with a flat tire and suspected drunk driving.

arguments.quote: To re‑emphasize the seriousness of offences associated with drunk driving, and as a caveat against trivializing them, I reproduce without reservation the comment made by Cory J. in R. v. Bernshaw, [1995] 1 S.C.R. 254: Every year, drunk driving leaves a terrible trail of death, injury, heartbreak and destruction. From the point of view of numbers alone, it has a far greater impact on Canadian society than any other crime. In terms of the deaths and serious injuries resulting in hospitalization, drunk driving is clearly the crime which causes the most significant social loss to the country.
arguments.claim: Drunk driving is a serious crime with significant social impact, as emphasized by Cory J. in R. v. Bernshaw.

arguments.quote: 42 The situation in Canada has improved since Cory J. made this damning observation, but only because both the authorities and society itself have made extensive efforts to raise public awareness and crack down on impaired driving. The vigilance and diligence of police forces have played a crucial role in this process. Both Assistant Director Rocheleau and retired officer Lapointe testified eloquently on this subject. It is clear from their testimony that Repentigny’s police force considers drunk driving offences to be very serious. Both these experienced police officers asserted that the attitude of the police has changed considerably over the years and that the days of tolerating and trivializing these offences are indeed over.
arguments.claim: Police vigilance and diligence have played a crucial role in reducing impaired driving in Canada.

arguments.quote: It is clear from their testimony that Repentigny’s police force considers drunk driving offences to be very serious. Both these experienced police officers asserted that the attitude of the police has changed considerably over the years and that the days of tolerating and trivializing these offences are indeed over.
arguments.claim: The police force in Repentigny considers drunk driving offences very serious and has changed its attitude over the years to no longer tolerate or trivialize these offences.

arguments.quote: 43 There are two points regarding the impact of the legal context on police discretion on which I am not in complete agreement with Doyon J.A. I will discuss, first, the administrative directives and, second, the distribution of responsibilities between the police and Crown prosecutors. 4.1.2.1 Administrative directives are not conclusive in determining intent to commit an offence 44 While the existence of administrative directives that apply to the situation in issue is far from being totally irrelevant, it cannot be as conclusive a factor as Doyon J.A. suggests. After quoting the passages from the police practices manual of Repentigny’s public safety service on the procedure to follow in impaired driving cases, he concluded as follows: [translation] In my opinion, these passages demonstrate the authorities’ clear intention that impaired driving offences should first be thoroughly investigated, although this does not preclude a subsequent decision not to prosecute. It must be noted that the period of time for taking breath samples is relatively short, which means that the investigation must be completed diligently and that this directive should be followed. A police officer who is familiar with such a directive and who has solemnly affirmed, under the Police Act (R.S.Q., c. P‑13.1), that he or she will perform the duties of his or her office honestly cannot be unaware of how serious the state considers this type of offence to be. In fact, the appellant’s superior officer himself concluded, after being informed of the events, that breath samples should have been taken.
arguments.claim: Administrative directives in the police practices manual are relevant but not conclusive in determining intent to commit an offence.

arguments.quote: 45 Doyon J.A. seems to be attributing to the administrative directives set out in the police practices manual a normative value that they do not have. It should be pointed out that these directives do not have the force of law. They therefore cannot alter the scope of a discretion that is founded in the common law or a statute. Section 254(2) of the Criminal Code is the only legislative provision that applies in the instant case and it gives peace officers the power, but does not impose on them a duty, to take breath samples. Thus, the police practices manual cannot transform the discretion to decide whether or not samples should be taken into a binding legal rule: Maple Lodge Farms Ltd. v. Government of Canada, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 2.
arguments.claim: The police practices manual directives do not have the force of law and cannot alter the scope of police discretion under the Criminal Code.

arguments.quote: In short, evidence of the existence of directives of this nature and evidence that the accused was, or is presumed to have been, aware of them at the time of the conduct in issue can shed light on the circumstances of the alleged exercise of his discretion. The same is true of evidence about the police service’s usual procedures, such as the testimony of Assistant Director Rocheleau and retired officer Lapointe in the case at bar. However, such evidence cannot be conclusive. 4.1.2.2 The distribution of responsibilities between Crown prosecutors and the police does not eliminate police discretion
arguments.claim: Evidence of administrative directives and usual police procedures can shed light on the exercise of discretion but cannot be conclusive.

arguments.quote: 47 Doyon J.A. also seems to suggest that, in Quebec, where it is a Crown prosecutor who authorizes the laying of criminal charges, Sergeant Beaudry’s discretionary power did not allow him to deal with Patrick Plourde’s case otherwise than by taking breath samples and arresting him.
arguments.claim: In Quebec, Crown prosecutors authorize criminal charges, but police discretion is not eliminated by this distribution of responsibilities.

arguments.quote: 48 With respect, I do not believe it is necessary to go that far. In my opinion, the proper functioning of the criminal justice system requires that all actors involved be able to exercise their judgment in performing their respective duties, even though one person’s discretion may overlap with that of another person. The police have a particular role to play in the criminal justice system, one that was initially founded in the common law, and it is important that they remain independent of the executive branch: R. v. Campbell, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 565, at paras. 27 to 36, and R. v. Regan, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 297, 2002 SCC 12. Doyon J.A.’s hierarchical vision according to which a police officer’s discretion is limited by the discretion of the Crown prosecutor should therefore be rejected. In discharging their respective duties, both the police officer and the prosecutor have a discretion that must be exercised independently of any outside influence: Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 372, 2002 SCC 65. The limits of each official’s discretion are inherent in that person’s role and duties. However, the responsibilities of Crown prosecutors do not serve to limit the scope of police discretion. 4.2 Relationship Between the Offence of Obstructing Justice and Police Discretion
arguments.claim: The proper functioning of the criminal justice system requires independent exercise of discretion by police and Crown prosecutors, even if their discretions overlap.

arguments.quote: Doyon J.A.’s hierarchical vision according to which a police officer’s discretion is limited by the discretion of the Crown prosecutor should therefore be rejected. In discharging their respective duties, both the police officer and the prosecutor have a discretion that must be exercised independently of any outside influence: Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 372, 2002 SCC 65. However, the responsibilities of Crown prosecutors do not serve to limit the scope of police discretion. 4.2 Relationship Between the Offence of Obstructing Justice and Police Discretion
arguments.claim: The police officer's discretion is not limited by the discretion of the Crown prosecutor and both must exercise their discretion independently.

arguments.quote: 49 As the trial judge aptly noted, the accused cannot be convicted of the offence provided for in s. 139(2) solely because he has exercised his discretion improperly.
arguments.claim: The accused cannot be convicted of obstructing justice solely because he exercised his discretion improperly.

arguments.quote: Therefore, it seems worth noting at the outset that, although they have some points in common, the review of the exercise of police discretion and the determination whether the offence of obstructing justice has been committed must not be confused. Although, in most cases, the evidence relied upon to establish that a course of conduct was not a proper exercise of the discretion can also be relied upon to establish the offence of obstructing justice, two separate analyses must perforce be conducted.
arguments.claim: Reviewing police discretion and determining whether obstructing justice has been committed are separate analyses, though they may rely on similar evidence.

arguments.quote: 50 In his dissenting reasons, Chamberland J.A. noted that, in the case at bar, the analyses of the actus reus and of the mens rea intersect, because both require that the honesty of the exercise of the discretion be considered.
arguments.claim: The actus reus and mens rea analyses intersect because both require considering the honesty of the exercise of discretion.

arguments.quote: However, the mere fact that there was no dishonest intention does not prove that the discretion has been exercised properly. The exercise of the discretion must also be justified on the basis of objective factors.
arguments.claim: Lack of dishonest intention does not prove proper exercise of discretion; it must also be justified on objective factors.

arguments.quote: In every case, it must be determined what a police officer acting reasonably would do in the same situation. It is necessary to identify those factors that in the eyes of an objective observer would justify the exercise of the discretion.
arguments.claim: The exercise of police discretion must be judged by what a reasonable police officer would do in the same situation, based on objective factors.

arguments.quote: Although one may assume that in most cases the underlying intention will be the decisive factor both for reviewing the exercise of the discretion and for determining whether there has been an obstruction of justice, it seems preferable to me to link the analysis of the exercise of the discretion with that of the actus reus.
arguments.claim: While intention is often decisive in reviewing discretion and determining obstruction, it is preferable to link discretion analysis with actus reus analysis.

arguments.quote: 54 It should first be noted that the trial judge made no error of law.
arguments.claim: The trial judge made no error of law.

arguments.quote: Judge Beaulieu began by clearly and unambiguously stating the principles applicable to the burden of proof and to his assessment of the credibility of the accused’s testimony.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu clearly stated the principles applicable to the burden of proof and assessed the credibility of the accused’s testimony.

arguments.quote: He then correctly described police discretion and its importance.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu correctly described police discretion and its importance.

arguments.quote: He also correctly delimited the scope of application of the criminal law and that of disciplinary law, by recognizing that an unjustified exercise of the discretion does not necessarily mean that the offence provided for in s. 139(2) has been committed.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu correctly delimited the scope of criminal law and disciplinary law, recognizing that unjustified exercise of discretion does not necessarily mean the offence in s. 139(2) was committed.

arguments.quote: Likewise, he correctly identified the constituent elements of the offence, including the need for the Crown to prove a specific intent to obstruct the course of justice.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu correctly identified the elements of the offence, including the need for the Crown to prove specific intent to obstruct justice.

arguments.quote: In short, Judge Beaulieu accurately stated the issue before him: [translation] In the case at bar, if the Court is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused decided not to have Plourde take a breathalyzer test because he was a Sûreté du Québec officer, a peace officer, and to give him a chance, that exercise of the discretion was unacceptable.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu accurately stated the issue before him as whether the accused decided not to have Plourde take a breathalyzer test because he was a peace officer, and that such an exercise of discretion was unacceptable.

arguments.quote: Fish J. relies on the following passage from Biniaris to assert that there is a “fundamental distinction between jury verdicts and verdicts rendered by trial judges” where the application of s. 686(1) (a)(i) is concerned: The Yebes test is expressed in terms of a verdict reached by a jury.
arguments.claim: Fish J. argues there is a fundamental distinction between jury verdicts and trial judge verdicts under s. 686(1)(a)(i), asserting the Yebes test applies only to jury verdicts.

arguments.quote: 57 Fish J. is correct in saying that a verdict can be unreasonable even if it can be supported by the evidence and that, in such a case, the court should order a new trial rather than entering an acquittal. This Court addressed this question as follows in R. v. Pittiman, [2006] 1 S.C.R. 381, 2006 SCC 9, at para. 14: Where a conviction is set aside on the ground that the verdict is unsupported by the evidence, the court of appeal, absent legal errors in respect of the admissibility of evidence, will usually enter an acquittal. However, where the verdict is found to be unreasonable on the basis of inconsistency of verdicts, but the evidence against the appellant supported the conviction, the appropriate remedy will usually be a new trial.
arguments.claim: Fish J. says a verdict can be unreasonable even if supported by evidence, and in such cases a new trial should be ordered rather than an acquittal.
arguments.outcome_note: Accepted that unreasonable verdicts may require new trials, but context matters.

arguments.quote: 59 In his analysis, Fish J. criticizes the trial judge for errors made in interpreting the evidence. He then finds that these errors were serious enough to require a new trial.
arguments.claim: Fish J. criticizes the trial judge for errors in interpreting evidence and finds them serious enough to require a new trial.

arguments.quote: The appellant submitted that once all the evidence is fairly assessed, no properly instructed trier of fact could reasonably have convicted him.
arguments.claim: The appellant submits that no properly instructed trier of fact could reasonably have convicted him after fairly assessing all evidence.

arguments.quote: 61 In his analysis, Fish J. does not consider all the evidence in determining whether the verdict is unreasonable. Hence, the reasoning that leads him to an order for a new trial seems to me rather to involve a finding under s. 686(1)(a)(iii) “that . . . on any ground there was a miscarriage of justice”. That is not the question before the Court.
arguments.claim: Fish J. does not consider all evidence in determining unreasonableness and seems to base his order for a new trial on miscarriage of justice under s. 686(1)(a)(iii), which is not the question before the Court.
arguments.outcome_note: Correct that miscarriage of justice is a different question than unreasonableness under s. 686(1)(a)(i).

arguments.quote: With respect, it is my view that Chamberland J.A. considered the latter question in his dissenting reasons. Moreover, his analysis does not take into account the trial judge’s privileged position in assessing the evidence.
arguments.claim: Chamberland J.A. considered whether a different verdict would have been reasonable, not the unreasonableness of the verdict, and did not account for the trial judge's privileged position.
arguments.outcome_note: Correct that Chamberland J.A.'s dissent focused on a different question and ignored trial judge's privilege.

arguments.quote: With respect, Fish J. does not take it into account either.
arguments.claim: Fish J. also failed to take into account the trial judge's privileged position in assessing evidence.
arguments.outcome_note: Correct that Fish J. did not respect trial judge's privileged position.

arguments.quote: The Crown submits that in deciding not to do so, he was obstructing justice, since he knew that this evidence was necessary to prove the offence alleged against Mr. Plourde under s. 253 of the Criminal Code .
arguments.claim: The Crown submits that Sergeant Beaudry was obstructing justice by deciding not to obtain breath samples, knowing that evidence was necessary to prove the offence under s. 253 of the Criminal Code.

arguments.quote: It is important to note that the charge is not based on an allegation that Sergeant Beaudry attempted to conceal the commission of an offence by Mr. Plourde.
arguments.claim: The charge is not based on an allegation that Sergeant Beaudry attempted to conceal the commission of an offence by Mr. Plourde.

arguments.quote: If I understand Fish J.’s reasons correctly, he concludes that the verdict is unreasonable, at least in part, because, in his view, there is no evidence capable of supporting a finding that Sergeant Beaudry attempted to conceal the fact that Mr. Plourde had committed an offence (see, inter alia, para. 111 of Fish J.’s reasons).
arguments.claim: Fish J. concludes the verdict is unreasonable partly because there is no evidence supporting a finding that Sergeant Beaudry attempted to conceal that Mr. Plourde committed an offence.
arguments.outcome_note: The issue is not concealment but the decision not to obtain breath samples.

arguments.quote: 65 In his analysis, Judge Beaulieu first described the facts that were relevant to the question whether Sergeant Beaudry’s decision constituted a proper exercise of his discretion. On this point, the evidence as a whole was such that it was reasonable to find that the circumstances were very serious. Admittedly, there were no accidents or injuries on the night in question. Nonetheless, there is no doubt that what took place before Sergeant Beaudry intervened was serious.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu described relevant facts and found the circumstances very serious despite no accidents or injuries.

arguments.quote: 66 Furthermore, although I do not agree completely with the weight Doyon J.A. gave to the administrative directives set out in the police practices manual, the fact remains that the directives, as well as the testimony of Assistant Director Rocheleau and retired officer Lapointe regarding the procedure normally followed in impaired driving cases, justifiably prompted the trial judge to require more convincing evidence in support of the claim that the discretion had been exercised for a humanitarian reason. As Doyon J.A., writing for the majority of the Court of Appeal, pointed out, [translation] “[i]n light of the seriousness of these circumstances, it was open to the judge to be circumspect, as he was, in considering [Sergeant Beaudry’s] version” (para. 71).
arguments.claim: The trial judge required more convincing evidence to support that discretion was exercised for humanitarian reasons, considering police directives and testimony about normal procedure.

arguments.quote: 67 The trial judge was also careful in weighing the testimony of the two officers, Constable Boucher and Constable Bélisle, who were with the accused on the night of September 22, 2000. Constable Boucher said that he had not taken the initiative to have Mr. Plourde take a breathalyzer test because he only suspected him of impaired driving. The appellant concedes that the judge correctly characterized that statement as a lie. Constable Bélisle stated that it was hard for him to say whether this was an impaired driving case. Once again, the judge made no error in finding that this was a lie. It was certainly open to the trial judge, in deciding whether the exercise of police discretion was appropriate in this case, to consider the testimony of the other officers who had also been in a position to assess the circumstances of the case. While only Sergeant Beaudry’s decision was in issue, the testimony of the other two officers was nonetheless important contextual evidence. That testimony was quite likely to enlighten the trial judge in his assessment of the situation the police had been dealing with that night. The fact that Sergeant Beaudry’s colleagues lied to the court cannot help but raise doubts about what really happened at the roadside, and subsequently at the police station.
arguments.claim: The trial judge carefully weighed testimony of officers Boucher and Bélisle, found their statements to be lies, and considered their testimony important contextual evidence.

arguments.quote: 68 Moreover, the trial judge noted that the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt that, even while at the roadside, the accused had remembered meeting the individual a little over a week earlier, on September 12, 2000. As of that point, therefore, he knew that he was dealing with a Sûreté du Québec officer. This finding is crucial, because it is the cornerstone of Judge Beaulieu’s verdict. Moreover, the evidence establishes that it was also at the roadside that Sergeant Beaudry decided not to follow the usual procedure.
arguments.claim: The trial judge found beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused knew at the roadside that Mr. Plourde was a Sûreté du Québec officer and decided not to follow usual procedure.

arguments.quote: 69 This, then, is the question on which the case turns, and Judge Beaulieu devoted the largest portion of his reasons to it. He believed the version of Sergeant Beaudry and his colleagues with respect to the description of Mr. Plourde himself and of Mr. Plourde’s conduct, but he was of the opinion that the [translation] “climate of distress” was raised after the fact to try to justify Sergeant Beaudry’s actions. The logic behind Judge Beaulieu’s finding that Alain Beaudry was guilty is clear. The main points of his reasoning are as follows.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu believed Sergeant Beaudry's version of Mr. Plourde's conduct but found the 'climate of distress' was raised after the fact to justify actions, leading to a finding of guilt.

arguments.quote: 70 Judge Beaulieu examined in detail Sergeant Beaudry’s claim that he had decided not to take breath samples because he wanted to help Mr. Plourde, knowing him to be depressed. However, the judge expressed scepticism regarding that explanation. To justify the decision he had made at the very scene of the incident, Sergeant Beaudry claimed to have recalled that Mr. Plourde’s depressive state had been discussed in the course of the interview on September 12, ten days earlier. Mr. Plourde, however, did not, in testifying, remember any discussion about this. Nor did the incident report written at the time mention it. In any event, the trial judge asked why Sergeant Beaudry had not taken Mr. Plourde to the hospital if he was so depressed that he posed a danger to himself. In the judge’s opinion, if the accused had been so worried about Mr. Plourde’s health, he should have ignored his refusal to go to the hospital, particularly when the accused expressly admitted in his testimony that it would have been preferable to take Mr. Plourde to the hospital. Judge Beaulieu also rightly observed that detaining Mr. Plourde in a room under video surveillance would have obviated the risk of a suicide attempt even if breath samples had been taken.
arguments.claim: Judge Beaulieu expressed scepticism about Sergeant Beaudry's claim that he decided not to take breath samples to help Mr. Plourde due to depression, noting lack of evidence and inconsistencies.

arguments.quote: 71 The trial judge also could not understand why Mr. Plourde’s depressive state was not mentioned anywhere in the file if that fact was so striking. For example, in his own activity log, the accused described Mr. Plourde as being in an advanced state of intoxication and noted that he had to “sleep it off”. It therefore seems that Sergeant Beaudry had inferred from the signs of distress exhibited by Mr. Plourde when he was stopped that he was drunk, not that he was depressed. The conclusion noted by Sergeant Beaudry, that Mr. Plourde was in an advanced state of intoxication, was perfectly reasonable, given the difficulty, to say the least, in distinguishing an abnormal mental state from a state of intoxication combined with the stress inherent in this kind of interaction with the police. The trial judge also could not have failed to notice that the handwritten memorandum stapled to the report prepared for Assistant Director Rocheleau did not mention depression or any other humanitarian reason, but referred only to the fact that Patrick Plourde was a police officer. This leads to the inexorable conclusion that more would be needed before a clinical diagnosis of severe depression or suicidal tendencies could be considered likely.
arguments.claim: The trial judge noted the absence of mention of depression in the file and concluded more evidence would be needed before considering a clinical diagnosis likely.

arguments.quote: 72 In addition to rejecting Sergeant Beaudry’s justifications based on humanitarian reasons, the trial judge also concluded, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the accused had acted knowingly and out of favouritism when he had failed to take timely breath samples.
arguments.claim: The trial judge concluded beyond a reasonable doubt that Sergeant Beaudry acted knowingly and out of favouritism when failing to take timely breath samples.

arguments.quote: On this point, Chamberland J.A. was of the opinion (at para. 55) that Sergeant Beaudry had acted transparently and that he had never attempted to conceal anything.
arguments.claim: Chamberland J.A. opined Sergeant Beaudry acted transparently and never attempted to conceal anything.
arguments.outcome_note: Trial judge's contrary conclusion was reasonable.

arguments.quote: 73 First, the trial judge believed Constable Dagenais’s testimony that when he had asked the accused whether he should obtain biometric information (photograph and fingerprints) from Mr. Plourde, the accused had replied that Mr. Plourde was under arrest for impaired driving. Here again, the trial judge was justified in wondering why the accused had not instead seen fit to explain to his colleague that Mr. Plourde had been brought to the police station for his own safety, because he was depressed and needed help more than anything else. The judge also believed Constable Dagenais when he added that Sergeant Beaudry had told him to wait because he had to make a decision. But Sergeant Beaudry had already decided to characterize the incident as an “unclassified” one. It was certainly open to the trial judge to conclude, unlike Chamberland J.A., that in acting in this way, the accused had not been candid.
arguments.claim: The trial judge believed Constable Dagenais's testimony that Sergeant Beaudry said Mr. Plourde was under arrest for impaired driving and had not been candid about the situation.

arguments.quote: 77 Quite apart from the merits of the appeal, however, Justice Fish urges the Court to reconsider the traditional scope of s. 686 (l)(a)(i) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 . In particular, Fish J. contends that an appellate court’s finding that a verdict is “unreasonable or cannot be supported by the evidence” should be available in a case where the verdict is dependent on findings of fact made by the trial judge “that are demonstrably incompatible . . . with evidence that is neither contradicted by other evidence nor rejected by the judge” (para. 98); in other words, in cases where on examination the substratum of findings on which the verdict rests disappears.
arguments.claim: Justice Fish urges the Court to reconsider the traditional scope of s. 686(1)(a)(i) of the Criminal Code to allow appellate courts to find a verdict unreasonable when it rests on trial judge's findings that are demonstrably incompatible with uncontradicted evidence.

arguments.quote: As she notes, the verdict turned on issues of credibility and “[t]he trial judge was in the best position to assess the credibility of the witnesses and to determine whether the evidence left room for a reasonable doubt” (para. 4).
arguments.claim: The verdict turned on credibility issues, and the trial judge was best positioned to assess witness credibility and determine if evidence left room for reasonable doubt.

arguments.quote: 78 As Charron J. points out, the law has traditionally focussed on the reasonableness of the verdict, not on the quality of the reasons given for reaching it.
arguments.claim: The law traditionally focuses on the reasonableness of the verdict, not on the quality of the reasons given for reaching it.

arguments.quote: Nevertheless, Charron J. accepts that “there may be a connection between an error made in interpreting evidence and an unreasonable verdict” (para. 59).
arguments.claim: There may be a connection between an error in interpreting evidence and an unreasonable verdict.

arguments.quote: The dissent in this case of Chamberland J.A. was not based on an “error of law” ([2005] R.J.Q. 2536, 2005 QCCA 966); accordingly, s. 686(1)(a)(ii), is not available to the appellant/accused here, even if it was thought to be applicable.
arguments.claim: The dissent in this case was not based on an error of law, so s. 686(1)(a)(ii) is not available to the appellant here.

arguments.quote: In the eyes of the litigants and the public, where the findings of facts essential to the verdict are “demonstrably incompatible” with evidence that is neither contradicted by other evidence nor rejected by the trial judge, such a verdict would lack legitimacy and would properly, I think, be treated as “unreasonable”.
arguments.claim: A verdict is unreasonable if the essential findings of fact are demonstrably incompatible with uncontradicted evidence not rejected by the trial judge, as such a verdict lacks legitimacy.

arguments.quote: In my view, with respect, the faults he has identified in the trial judge’s reasons have neither the centrality to the verdict nor the incompatibility with the record sufficient to justify a reversal.
arguments.claim: The faults identified in the trial judge's reasons do not have the centrality to the verdict nor incompatibility with the record sufficient to justify reversal.

arguments.quote: 81 A police officer is entitled, like any other accused, to be presumed innocent until reasonably and properly convicted — even when another officer is the beneficiary of the alleged offence.
arguments.claim: A police officer is entitled to be presumed innocent until reasonably and properly convicted, even if the alleged offence benefits another officer.

arguments.quote: 83 The decisive question at trial was whether Mr. Beaudry had refrained from asking for that sample because Mr. Plourde was a police officer.
arguments.claim: The decisive question was whether Beaudry refrained from asking for the sample because the arrested person was a police officer, and the trial judge answered affirmatively.

arguments.quote: In my respectful view it is, because the judge’s conclusions are not supported by the reasons upon which he caused them to rest — and because his reasons are fundamentally incompatible with the uncontradicted evidence at trial.
arguments.claim: The trial judge's conclusions are not supported by the reasons and are fundamentally incompatible with the uncontradicted evidence, making the verdict unreasonable under s. 686(1)(a)(i).

arguments.quote: 85 I agree with Justice Charron’s analysis of s. 139(2) of the Criminal Code . More particularly, I agree that the actus reus and the mens rea for obstruction of justice should not be conflated. An improper exercise of discretion will amount to an obstruction of justice only when it is accompanied by an intent to “obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice”.
arguments.claim: The actus reus and mens rea for obstruction of justice should not be conflated; improper discretion amounts to obstruction only with intent to obstruct justice.

arguments.quote: Mr. Beaudry must thus be shown to have acted corruptly or dishonestly — that is, beyond the scope of what he believed to be within his lawful discretion as a police officer.
arguments.claim: Beaudry must be shown to have acted corruptly or dishonestly, beyond lawful discretion as a police officer, to be guilty of obstruction of justice.

arguments.quote: 86 Like Justice Charron, I believe that police discretion is an essential element of the justice system in Quebec, as in other provinces. It is neither narrowed by the attorney general’s authority to press charges independently of a police recommendation, nor displaced by the provisions of internal police directives.
arguments.claim: Police discretion is an essential element of the justice system in Quebec and other provinces, and it is not limited by the attorney general's authority or internal police directives.

arguments.quote: 96 In short, the text of the governing provision of the Criminal Code and its recent application by the Court suggest that, at least in non-jury cases, appellate courts may find a verdict to be unreasonable even where the verdict was available on the record.
arguments.claim: Appellate courts may find a verdict unreasonable even if it was available on the record, especially in non-jury cases.

arguments.quote: 97 In Justice Charron’s view, a verdict based on unreasonable reasons is not unreasonable if there is evidence upon which another trier of fact could have reached the same conclusion by a different and proper route.
arguments.claim: A verdict based on unreasonable reasons is not unreasonable if another trier of fact could have reached the same conclusion by a different and proper route.

arguments.quote: I think it preferable by far, where there is evidence capable of supporting a conviction, to order a new trial so that a fresh and proper determination can be made by a real and not hypothetical “other judge”.
arguments.claim: Where evidence supports a conviction, it is preferable to order a new trial for a fresh determination by a real judge rather than uphold a verdict based on illogical reasons.

arguments.quote: 99 The trial judge’s findings of fact can be fairly summarized this way: (1) Neither of the officers who were with the appellant at the time of the incident are credible witnesses because they both denied having anything more than a suspicion that Mr. Plourde was intoxicated when he was first pulled over;
arguments.claim: The trial judge found the officers with the appellant not credible because they denied suspicion of intoxication when first stopping Mr. Plourde.

arguments.quote: (2) The appellant’s decision to classify the incident as [translation] “assistance to the public” and “unclassified activity”, though he knew that Mr. Plourde was driving while intoxicated, indicates that he was trying to hide that fact; (3) The appellant’s contention that he believed Mr. Plourde was depressed and in need of help is not true.
arguments.claim: The trial judge found the appellant tried to hide that Mr. Plourde was driving intoxicated by classifying the incident as assistance to the public and unclassified activity.

arguments.quote: Had the appellant really believed that Mr. Plourde was depressed, he would have taken him to the hospital and not to the police station. Moreover, the police report did not indicate that Mr. Plourde was depressed; rather, the woman who accused Mr. Plourde of harassment in the incident ten days prior referred to Mr. Plourde as being [translation] “mentally disturbed” (not “depressed”) and the report on that incident used the same words.
arguments.claim: The trial judge found the appellant's claim that he believed Mr. Plourde was depressed and needed help was untrue, as he would have taken him to hospital otherwise and the police report did not indicate depression.

arguments.quote: Finally, Mr. Plourde himself testified that he did not recall the issue being raised with the appellant; and (4) The testimony of Raymond Dagenais and Marc Rocheleau carried much weight.
arguments.claim: Mr. Plourde did not recall the issue of depression being raised with the appellant.

arguments.quote: Finally, Mr. Plourde himself testified that he did not recall the issue being raised with the appellant; and (4) The testimony of Raymond Dagenais and Marc Rocheleau carried much weight.
arguments.claim: The testimony of Raymond Dagenais and Marc Rocheleau was given much weight by the trial judge.

arguments.quote: Dagenais testified that the appellant told him that Mr. Plourde was under arrest but that Dagenais should not photograph him yet because [translation] “he had a decision to make”.
arguments.claim: Dagenais testified the appellant said Mr. Plourde was under arrest but delayed photographing him because he had a decision to make.

arguments.quote: Rocheleau testified that the appellant told him that [translation] “[w]e’ve exercised our discretion to give a chance.”
arguments.claim: Rocheleau testified the appellant said they exercised discretion to give Mr. Plourde a chance.

arguments.quote: 100 On this basis, the trial judge concluded that the appellant attempted to conceal that Mr. Plourde had driven a motor vehicle while intoxicated and thus to preclude the laying of charges against him.
arguments.claim: The trial judge concluded the appellant tried to conceal that Mr. Plourde had driven intoxicated to prevent charges being laid.

arguments.quote: The judge found as well that the appellant had improperly exercised his discretion in failing to subject Mr. Plourde to a breathalyzer test and in declining to recommend that he be prosecuted (whether to prosecute was not for the appellant to decide).
arguments.claim: The trial judge found the appellant improperly exercised discretion by not administering a breathalyzer and not recommending prosecution, which was not his decision to make.

arguments.quote: In the judge’s view, the appellant had acted out of favouritism for a fellow police officer and not because he believed that Mr. Plourde was depressed and in need of help.
arguments.claim: The trial judge found the appellant acted out of favouritism for a fellow officer, not because he believed Mr. Plourde was depressed and needed help.

arguments.quote: 101 In my respectful view, this is a case where the trial judge’s reasons suffer, in the language of Biniaris, from flaws in the evaluation and analysis of the evidence that justify reversal (para. 37). This is particularly true with regard to the only real issue in the case — whether the appellant had acted corruptly or dishonestly, with the requisite intent to obstruct justice.
arguments.claim: The trial judge's reasons suffer from flaws in evaluating and analyzing evidence that justify reversal, especially regarding whether the appellant acted corruptly or dishonestly with intent to obstruct justice.

arguments.quote: 102 I defer to the trial judge’s adverse conclusion as to the credibility of officers Boucher and Bélisle. In any event, their testimony is hardly decisive. Whether or not they immediately had reasonable grounds to suspect that Mr. Plourde was drunk does not bear on the critical issues: Did the appellant exercise his discretion in good faith or with intent to obstruct justice?
arguments.claim: The credibility findings against officers Boucher and Bélisle are accepted but their testimony is not decisive on whether the appellant acted in good faith or to obstruct justice.

arguments.quote: Did the appellant refrain from arresting Mr. Plourde and administering the alcohol test because he believed Mr. Plourde was depressed and in need of help or because he wanted to shield a fellow police officer from criminal proceedings?
arguments.claim: The critical issue is whether the appellant refrained from arresting and testing Mr. Plourde because he believed he was depressed and needed help or to shield a fellow officer from criminal proceedings.

arguments.quote: 103 I now turn to the trial judge’s other findings which are more relevant to this issue.
arguments.claim: The trial judge's other findings are more relevant to the issue of intent to obstruct justice.

arguments.quote: 104 With respect to the police reports, the trial judge stated: [translation] The Court has taken into consideration the writing of the incident report and the memorandum prepared by the accused and stapled to the report, which was left in Rocheleau’s pigeonhole.
arguments.claim: The trial judge considered the incident report and memorandum prepared by the appellant, which were intended to divert attention from the night's events.

arguments.quote: Even the Crown conceded that the appellant did in fact offer to take Mr. Plourde to the hospital but to no avail: Mr. Plourde refused to go.
arguments.claim: The Crown conceded that the appellant did offer to take Mr. Plourde to the hospital but Mr. Plourde refused to go.

arguments.quote: The judge stated: [translation] Marc Rocheleau, the assistant director, is a very credible witness. The Court believes his account of the comments the accused made to him, including the following: “We’ve exercised our discretion to give a chance.”
arguments.claim: The trial judge found Marc Rocheleau to be a very credible witness and believed his account of the accused's comments including 'We've exercised our discretion to give a chance.'

arguments.quote: There is no dispute that the appellant had made a conscious decision to help rather than charge Mr. Plourde. The question was whether he was motivated by a sense of camaraderie or by compassion, misguided or not.
arguments.claim: The appellant made a conscious decision to help rather than charge Mr. Plourde, but the question is whether this was motivated by camaraderie or compassion.

holdings.quote: The accused, a police officer, was charged with obstructing justice under s. 139(2) of the Criminal Code for deliberately failing to gather the evidence needed to lay criminal charges against P, another police officer, who he had reasonable grounds to believe had been operating a motor vehicle while intoxicated. 1 Charron J. — The appellant police officer, Alain Beaudry, is charged with obstructing justice under s. 139(2) of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C‑46 . It is alleged that he deliberately failed to gather the evidence needed to lay criminal charges against a suspect who he had reasonable grounds to believe had been operating a motor vehicle while intoxicated.
holdings.statement: Alain Beaudry is the appellant police officer charged with obstructing justice under s. 139(2) of the Criminal Code for deliberately failing to gather evidence to lay charges against another police officer suspected of impaired driving.

holdings.quote: Mr. Beaudry has appealed to this Court as of right.
holdings.statement: Mr. Beaudry appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada as of right.

holdings.quote: I would therefore dismiss the appeal.
holdings.statement: The appeal should be dismissed because the verdict was reasonable.

holdings.quote: 5 At the time of the events that led to this appeal, Alain Beaudry was an officer — a sergent chargé de la relève (shift supervisor) — of the police service of the city of Repentigny.
holdings.statement: Alain Beaudry was a sergeant and shift supervisor with the Repentigny police service at the time of the events.

holdings.quote: On September 22, 2000, at about 3:30 a.m., Sergeant Beaudry was assisting Constable Martin Boucher and Constable Hugo Bélisle in a routine operation when they heard a vehicle coming toward them making an unusual noise, as if it was running on a flat tire. Taking the lead, Sergeant Beaudry returned to his patrol car and set off in pursuit of the vehicle, followed closely by his two colleagues. At that point, Sergeant Beaudry estimated that the vehicle, a minivan, was travelling at between 60 and 70 km/h, which was over the speed limit. He also had the impression that it was a stolen vehicle.
holdings.statement: On September 22, 2000, Sergeant Beaudry pursued a minivan suspected of speeding and possibly stolen.

holdings.quote: Constable Boucher testified that, during the pursuit, the driver of the minivan drove through a stop sign and almost hit the median.
holdings.statement: Constable Boucher testified that the minivan ran a stop sign and nearly hit the median during the pursuit.

holdings.quote: Sergeant Beaudry communicated with the dispatcher at the police station, who told him that the vehicle had not been reported stolen and that it belonged to a resident of Repentigny named Patrick Plourde.
holdings.statement: The dispatcher informed Sergeant Beaudry that the vehicle was not reported stolen and belonged to Patrick Plourde.

holdings.quote: 6 When the minivan finally stopped, Sergeant Beaudry was the first officer to approach the vehicle.
holdings.statement: When the minivan stopped, Sergeant Beaudry was the first officer to approach the vehicle.

holdings.quote: The driver of the vehicle did not seem to pay much attention to Sergeant Beaudry, as he was trying to restrain a German shepherd inside the vehicle.
