Sergeant Beaudry ordered him, several times, to keep his hands on the steering wheel. The driver did not respond, but began to bang his head on the wheel.
holdings.statement: The driver was distracted trying to restrain a German shepherd and did not respond to orders to keep his hands on the steering wheel.

holdings.quote: Sergeant Beaudry approached the vehicle and tried to speak with the driver, who was crying and talking in a confused manner. He also asked the driver whether he wanted to be taken to the hospital and to have someone look after his dog. This elicited no response either.
holdings.statement: Sergeant Beaudry tried to speak with the driver, who was crying and confused, and offered hospital assistance and care for the dog, but received no response.

holdings.quote: After a few minutes, the driver got out of the vehicle and threw himself on the ground. While the police were helping him up, Mr. Plourde said, [translation] “I do the same job as you do”, and showed them his police badge.
holdings.statement: The driver got out of the vehicle and threw himself on the ground, then identified himself as a police officer named Patrick Plourde.

holdings.quote: 7 At that point, Sergeant Beaudry remembered that he had met Constable Patrick Plourde about ten days earlier, when a colleague had asked him to act as a witness to a conversation he was having with a woman and Mr. Plourde. Although the woman did not want to file a complaint against Mr. Plourde, she wanted to warn him that she was not going to put up any more with his incessant telephone calls and threats to have his fellow police officers give her tickets if she kept refusing to date him.
holdings.statement: Sergeant Beaudry recalled meeting Constable Patrick Plourde about ten days earlier during a conversation involving a woman who complained about Plourde's behavior and threats.

holdings.quote: According to Sergeant Beaudry, she also said that she knew Mr. Plourde was depressed and was being treated by a physician. According to Mr. Plourde, however, the matter had not been raised.
holdings.statement: The woman said Plourde was depressed and being treated by a physician, but Plourde denied this.

holdings.quote: The occurrence report prepared by Constable Simard and countersigned by Sergeant Beaudry notes that the woman claimed that Mr. Plourde was [translation] “mentally disturbed”.
holdings.statement: An occurrence report noted the woman claimed Plourde was mentally disturbed.

holdings.quote: 8 After Mr. Plourde was back on his feet, the officers took him to the patrol car of Constable Boucher and Constable Bélisle. Mr. Plourde then banged his head several times on the hood of the vehicle, and the officers decided to handcuff him.
holdings.statement: After being helped up, Plourde banged his head on the patrol car hood and was handcuffed after resisting.

holdings.quote: He resisted, and it was while trying to get him under control that Sergeant Beaudry and his two colleagues first smelled alcohol. On cross‑examination, Sergeant Beaudry expressly acknowledged that this was when he suspected Mr. Plourde of driving while impaired.
holdings.statement: Sergeant Beaudry and colleagues first smelled alcohol while trying to control Plourde, leading to suspicion of impaired driving.

holdings.quote: Mr. Plourde was then taken to the Repentigny police station in the vehicle of Constable Bélisle and Constable Boucher.
holdings.statement: Plourde was taken to the Repentigny police station in the patrol car.

holdings.quote: 9 While Sergeant Beaudry was en route to the station, the dispatcher asked him how to classify the occurrence. He told her: [translation] “Enter it as ‘Assistance to the public’ for now.”
holdings.statement: While en route to the station, Sergeant Beaudry told the dispatcher to classify the occurrence as 'Assistance to the public' for the time being.

holdings.quote: He testified that when he arrived at the station, he went to see Mr. Plourde, who was still sitting in the back seat of the patrol car. He offered once again to take him to the hospital, but Mr. Plourde refused. Mr. Plourde did not want anyone to be asked to come and pick him up either.
holdings.statement: At the station, Sergeant Beaudry offered to take Plourde to the hospital again, but Plourde refused and did not want anyone to pick him up.

holdings.quote: Sergeant Beaudry decided to put him in the youth detention room to let him calm down. He testified that it was at this moment, when he saw Mr. Plourde staggering, that he had reasonable and probable grounds to believe that Mr. Plourde had in fact committed the offence of driving while impaired.
holdings.statement: Sergeant Beaudry decided to put Plourde in the youth detention room to calm down and at that moment had reasonable grounds to believe Plourde had committed impaired driving.

holdings.quote: 10 This was also when he decided not to demand that Mr. Plourde take a breathalyzer test. He felt that Mr. Plourde was depressed and that he needed treatment.
holdings.statement: Sergeant Beaudry decided not to demand a breathalyzer test because he felt Plourde was depressed and needed treatment.

holdings.quote: I would note in passing that it is uncontested that a qualified breathalyzer technician — Constable Boucher — was present and that samples could accordingly have been taken within the time provided for by law.
holdings.statement: It was uncontested that a qualified breathalyzer technician was present and samples could have been taken within the legal time.

holdings.quote: 11 Later, Constable Boucher asked Sergeant Beaudry whether he should prepare an occurrence report. Sergeant Beaudry said yes. After looking at the list of occurrence codes, he told Constable Boucher to use the code for [translation] “unclassified activity”.
holdings.statement: Constable Boucher asked Sergeant Beaudry whether to prepare an occurrence report, and Beaudry agreed and instructed to use the code for 'unclassified activity'.

holdings.quote: Constable Boucher’s report, which Sergeant Beaudry later countersigned, mentions, among other things, that Mr. Plourde was in an advanced state of intoxication. Sergeant Beaudry attached to his report a memorandum to Assistant Director Rocheleau stating that Patrick Plourde was an officer of the Sûreté du Québec and that his immediate superior might have to be contacted.
holdings.statement: The occurrence report mentioned Plourde was in an advanced state of intoxication and Beaudry attached a memorandum noting Plourde was a Sûreté du Québec officer whose superior might need to be contacted.

holdings.quote: Sergeant Beaudry replied that he had exercised his discretion and decided neither to arrest Mr. Plourde nor to have him take a breathalyzer test. He explained that in his opinion Mr. Plourde was more in need of a helping hand than a blow to the head.
holdings.statement: Sergeant Beaudry exercised his discretion not to arrest Mr. Plourde or have him take a breathalyzer test, believing Mr. Plourde needed help rather than punishment.

holdings.quote: 16 According to Judge Beaulieu, when a peace officer claims to have exercised his or her discretion as in the present case, the court must determine the underlying intention of the exercise of the discretion in order to ascertain whether the peace officer exercised it honestly, and not arbitrarily, out of favouritism or with any other dishonest intention.
holdings.statement: When a peace officer claims to have exercised discretion, the court must determine if it was exercised honestly and not arbitrarily, out of favouritism or dishonesty.

holdings.quote: 38 The required justification is essentially twofold. First, the exercise of the discretion must be justified subjectively, that is, the discretion must have been exercised honestly and transparently, and on the basis of valid and reasonable grounds (reasons of Chamberland J.A., at para. 41). Thus, a decision based on favouritism, or on cultural, social or racial stereotypes, cannot constitute a proper exercise of police discretion.
holdings.statement: The exercise of police discretion must be justified subjectively by honesty, transparency, and valid, reasonable grounds, and cannot be based on favouritism or stereotypes.

holdings.quote: 39 Hence, the exercise of police discretion must also be justified on the basis of objective factors. I agree with Doyon J.A. that in determining whether a decision resulting from an exercise of police discretion is proper, it is important to consider the material circumstances in which the discretion was exercised.
holdings.statement: Police discretion must also be justified on objective factors, including the material circumstances in which the discretion was exercised.

holdings.quote: 40 First, it is self‑evident that the material circumstances are an important factor in the assessment of a police officer’s decision: the discretion will certainly not be exercised in the same way in a case of shoplifting by a teenager as one involving a robbery.
holdings.statement: Material circumstances are important in assessing police discretion; discretion will differ depending on the seriousness of the offence.

holdings.quote: 51 Where the discretionary power is relied upon, the analysis of the actus reus of the offence must therefore be carried out in two stages.
holdings.statement: The analysis of the actus reus of the offence when police discretion is relied upon must be carried out in two stages.

holdings.quote: First, it must be determined whether the conduct in issue can be regarded as a proper exercise of police discretion.
holdings.statement: First, it must be determined whether the conduct in issue can be regarded as a proper exercise of police discretion.

holdings.quote: If, beyond a reasonable doubt, the conduct in issue cannot constitute a proper exercise of police discretion, the analysis must be pursued further.
holdings.statement: If beyond a reasonable doubt the conduct cannot constitute a proper exercise of police discretion, the analysis must be pursued further.

holdings.quote: 52 Second, it must be determined whether the offence of obstructing justice, the parameters of which are well established, has been committed.
holdings.statement: Second, it must be determined whether the offence of obstructing justice has been committed, with well-established parameters.

holdings.quote: To sum up, the actus reus of the offence will be established only if the act tended to defeat or obstruct the course of justice (R. v. May (1984), 13 C.C.C. (3d) 257 (Ont. C.A.), per Martin J.A.; see also R. v. Hearn (1989), 48 C.C.C. (3d) 376 (Nfld. C.A.), per Goodridge C.J.N., aff’d [1989] 2 S.C.R. 1180).
holdings.statement: The actus reus of obstructing justice is established only if the act tended to defeat or obstruct the course of justice.

holdings.quote: With respect to mens rea, it is not in dispute that this is a specific intent offence (R. v. Charbonneau (1992), 13 C.R. (4th) 191 (Que. C.A.)). The prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused did in fact intend to act in a way tending to obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice.
holdings.statement: Obstructing justice is a specific intent offence requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended to act in a way tending to obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice.

holdings.quote: A simple error of judgment will not be enough.
holdings.statement: A simple error of judgment is not enough to constitute obstructing justice.

holdings.quote: An accused who acted in good faith, but whose conduct cannot be characterized as a legitimate exercise of the discretion, has not committed the criminal offence of obstructing justice.
holdings.statement: An accused who acted in good faith but whose conduct cannot be characterized as a legitimate exercise of discretion has not committed the criminal offence of obstructing justice.

holdings.quote: However, this appeal raises only one question of law: whether the verdict of Judge Beaulieu of the Court of Québec was unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The appeal raises only one question of law: whether the verdict of Judge Beaulieu was unreasonable.

holdings.quote: 55 I agree with the majority of the Court of Appeal that it was reasonable for the trial judge to find that the accused had breached his duty by giving preferential treatment to Mr. Plourde because he was a peace officer.
holdings.statement: It was reasonable for the trial judge to find that the accused breached his duty by giving preferential treatment to Mr. Plourde because he was a peace officer.

holdings.quote: The standard to be applied in reviewing a verdict was established in R. v. Yebes, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 168, and R. v. Biniaris, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 381, 2000 SCC 15, and it is not in issue in this appeal. In Biniaris, Arbour J. summarized it as follows: The test for an appellate court determining whether the verdict of a jury or the judgment of a trial judge is unreasonable or cannot be supported by the evidence has been unequivocally expressed in Yebes as follows: [C]urial review is invited whenever a jury goes beyond a reasonable standard. . . . [T]he test is “whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury acting judicially, could reasonably have rendered”. (Yebes, supra, at p. 185 (quoting Corbett v. The Queen, [1975] 2 S.C.R. 275, at p. 282, per Pigeon J.).)
holdings.statement: The standard for reviewing a verdict is whether a properly instructed jury acting judicially could reasonably have rendered the verdict, as established in R. v. Yebes and R. v. Biniaris.

holdings.quote: That formulation of the test imports both an objective assessment and, to some extent, a subjective one. It requires the appeal court to determine what verdict a reasonable jury, properly instructed, could judicially have arrived at, and, in doing so, to review, analyse and, within the limits of appellate disadvantage, weigh the evidence.
holdings.statement: The test for unreasonableness involves both an objective and somewhat subjective assessment, requiring the appellate court to determine what verdict a reasonable jury could judicially have arrived at, reviewing and weighing the evidence within appellate limits.

holdings.quote: This Court addressed this question as follows in R. v. Pittiman, [2006] 1 S.C.R. 381, 2006 SCC 9, at para. 14: Where a conviction is set aside on the ground that the verdict is unsupported by the evidence, the court of appeal, absent legal errors in respect of the admissibility of evidence, will usually enter an acquittal. C.A.), at para. 30, “[a]n acquittal is the appropriate order because it would be unfair to order a new trial and give the Crown a second opportunity to present a case on which a reasonable trier of fact could convict.” However, where the verdict is found to be unreasonable on the basis of inconsistency of verdicts, but the evidence against the appellant supported the conviction, the appropriate remedy will usually be a new trial.
holdings.statement: Where a verdict is unsupported by evidence, an acquittal is usually entered; but where unreasonableness arises from inconsistent verdicts with supporting evidence, a new trial is usually appropriate.

holdings.quote: 58 However, it must not be forgotten that, as Arbour J. clearly indicated, the Yebes test does not vary depending on whether the trial is a jury or a non-jury trial. The test to be applied is “whether the verdict is one that a properly instructed jury acting judicially, could reasonably have rendered”.
holdings.statement: The Yebes test does not vary between jury and non-jury trials; the focus is on whether a properly instructed jury could reasonably have rendered the verdict.

holdings.quote: In every case, it is the conclusion that is reviewed, not the process followed to reach it. I agree that, as Arbour J. explained in the passage quoted above, errors or a faulty thought process in a judge’s reasons can sometimes explain an unreasonable conclusion reached by the judge. But a verdict is not necessarily unreasonable because the judge has made errors in his or her analysis.
holdings.statement: The appellate review focuses on the conclusion, not the process, and errors in a judge's reasoning do not necessarily make a verdict unreasonable.

holdings.quote: The review must go further than that. In every case, the court must determine whether the verdict is unreasonable and, to do so, it must consider all the evidence. Arbour J. explained this as follows in R. v. A.G., [2000] 1 S.C.R. 439, 2000 SCC 17: In embarking on the exercise mandated by s. 686(1) (a)(i) of the Criminal Code , the reviewing court must engage in a thorough re-examination of the evidence and bring to bear the weight of its judicial experience to decide whether, on all the evidence, the verdict was a reasonable one.
holdings.statement: The court must consider all the evidence to determine if the verdict is unreasonable, engaging in a thorough re-examination and applying judicial experience.

holdings.quote: Doherty J.A. of the Ontario Court of Appeal explained this well in R. v. Morrissey (1995), 97 C.C.C. (3d) 193, as follows: A misapprehension of the evidence does not render a verdict unreasonable. Nor is a finding that the judge misapprehended the evidence a condition precedent to a finding that a verdict is unreasonable. In cases tried without juries, a finding that the trial judge did misapprehend the evidence can, however, figure prominently in an argument that the resulting verdict was unreasonable. An appellant will be in a much better position to demonstrate the unreasonableness of a verdict if the appellant can demonstrate that the trial judge misapprehended significant evidence . . . .
holdings.statement: A misapprehension of evidence does not automatically render a verdict unreasonable, nor is it a prerequisite to finding unreasonableness, though it can support such an argument in non-jury trials.

holdings.quote: 60 Thus, it is not enough to determine that the trial judge made errors. The analysis must be taken further. Laskin J.A. of the Ontario Court of Appeal summarized the analysis as follows in R. v. G. (G.) (1995), 97 C.C.C. (3d) 362: When an appellate court finds error, it has a duty to consider the nature of the error, its effect on the verdict, and when the verdict is rendered by a judge alone, on the reasoning process by which the verdict was reached.
holdings.statement: It is not enough to find errors; the appellate court must consider the nature and effect of errors on the verdict and the reasoning process when the verdict is by a judge alone.

holdings.quote: Obviously, not every error in the apprehension or appreciation of evidence or in the drawing of a conclusion from the evidence warrants quashing a conviction. But s. 686(1)(a) of the Criminal Code requires this court to intervene if the error leads to an unreasonable verdict, or if the error is an error of law which cannot be cured by s. 686(1) (b)(iii), or if the error results in a miscarriage of justice.
holdings.statement: Not every error in evidence appreciation warrants quashing a conviction, but s. 686(1)(a) requires intervention if the error leads to an unreasonable verdict, an incurable legal error, or a miscarriage of justice.

holdings.quote: I do not think this is a tenable submission. A.G.’s evidence did not legally require corroboration. Her evidence, even in the context of the other evidence in this case, was evidence which could reasonably support the appellant’s conviction. Therefore, I cannot say the verdict was unreasonable.
holdings.statement: The appellant's submission is untenable because the evidence, including A.G.'s, could reasonably support the conviction and did not legally require corroboration.

holdings.quote: Moreover, the question whether the judge misapprehended the evidence to such an extent that there was a miscarriage of justice is a mixed question of fact and law. An appellate court that considers a question such as this must bear in mind the privileged position of the trial judge.
holdings.statement: Whether the judge misapprehended evidence to the extent of miscarriage of justice is a mixed question of fact and law, and appellate courts must respect the trial judge's privileged position.

holdings.quote: 62 I readily appreciate that the deference owed to a trial court’s findings of fact must not become a pretext for an appellate court to evade its responsibility to set aside an unreasonable verdict. This is why no finding of fact is entirely exempt from appellate court scrutiny. Nonetheless, as this Court has consistently said, the integrity of our judicial system requires that the trial judge’s privileged position in assessing the facts be respected.
holdings.statement: Deference to trial court findings must not prevent appellate courts from setting aside unreasonable verdicts, but trial judges' privileged position in assessing facts must be respected.

holdings.quote: It should also be borne in mind that the question whether a verdict is unreasonable is not the same as the question whether a different verdict would have been reasonable had the evidence presented at trial been interpreted differently.
holdings.statement: The question whether a verdict is unreasonable is distinct from whether a different verdict would have been reasonable if evidence had been interpreted differently.

holdings.quote: That is why in R. v. Burke, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 474, Sopinka J. stated that the appellate courts’ power of review must be exercised sparingly when the verdict rests on a question of credibility (paras. 5-6). He added that instances where a trial court’s assessment of credibility cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence were “rare” (para. 7).
holdings.statement: Appellate courts must exercise their power of review sparingly when the verdict rests on a question of credibility, as such instances where a trial court's assessment of credibility cannot be supported on any reasonable view of the evidence are rare.

holdings.quote: It is therefore with this caveat in mind that I will now consider Judge Beaulieu’s interpretation of the evidence.
holdings.statement: The trial judge's interpretation of the evidence regarding credibility is considered with the caveat that appellate review on credibility is limited.

holdings.quote: 64 There is no doubt that Mr. Plourde was operating his vehicle while intoxicated, and indeed in an advanced state of intoxication.
holdings.statement: Mr. Plourde was operating his vehicle while intoxicated, in an advanced state of intoxication.

holdings.quote: It has also been clearly established that Sergeant Beaudry decided not to gather the evidence that would have been needed in order to lay criminal charges. The charge against Sergeant Beaudry is in fact based on his decision not to obtain breath samples.
holdings.statement: Sergeant Beaudry decided not to gather evidence needed to lay criminal charges, specifically not obtaining breath samples.

holdings.quote: What is in fact in issue is Sergeant Beaudry’s decision not to obtain breath samples. In the present case, was this an acceptable exercise of police discretion? If not, did it constitute an obstruction of the course of justice?
holdings.statement: The issue is whether Sergeant Beaudry's decision not to obtain breath samples was an acceptable exercise of police discretion and if not, whether it constituted obstruction of justice.

holdings.quote: Patrick Plourde was speeding and was driving on a public roadway with a flat tire, and he failed to make a stop and just missed the median. Then, when the police gave chase, he continued along his way for some distance before bringing his vehicle to a stop. After pulling over, he ignored Sergeant Beaudry for several minutes, sat with his head down on the wheel, cried, spoke in a confused manner, and fell down when he got out of his vehicle.
holdings.statement: Patrick Plourde was speeding, driving with a flat tire, failed to stop, and after police chase, stopped his vehicle but behaved confusedly and fell down.

holdings.quote: The fact that Sergeant Beaudry’s colleagues lied to the court cannot help but raise doubts about what really happened at the roadside, and subsequently at the police station.
holdings.statement: The lies of Sergeant Beaudry's colleagues raised doubts about what really happened at the roadside and police station.

holdings.quote: There are thus two possibilities: Sergeant Beaudry decided not to pursue the investigation either out of favouritism because Mr. Plourde was a peace officer, or because he knew that Mr. Plourde was depressed and needed help. The parties agree that if Sergeant Beaudry acted out of favouritism he is guilty of the offence with which he is charged.
holdings.statement: The case turns on whether Sergeant Beaudry acted out of favouritism or humanitarian reasons in deciding not to pursue the investigation.

holdings.quote: 74 Accordingly, these findings of fact, particularly with respect to Sergeant Beaudry’s credibility, provide ample support for the judge’s conclusion that on September 22, 2000, Sergeant Beaudry acted out of favouritism and had the specific intent to obstruct, pervert or defeat the course of justice by not taking the breath samples that would have been needed to lay a charge against Patrick Plourde under s. 253 of the Criminal Code .
holdings.statement: The trial judge's findings on Sergeant Beaudry's credibility support the conclusion that he acted out of favouritism with intent to obstruct justice by not taking breath samples needed to lay charges.

holdings.quote: 75 For these reasons, I find that Judge Beaulieu’s verdict was not unreasonable and I would dismiss the appeal.
holdings.statement: Judge Beaulieu's verdict was not unreasonable.

holdings.quote: 75 For these reasons, I find that Judge Beaulieu’s verdict was not unreasonable and I would dismiss the appeal.
holdings.statement: The appeal is dismissed.

holdings.quote: In particular, Fish J. contends that an appellate court’s finding that a verdict is “unreasonable or cannot be supported by the evidence” should be available in a case where the verdict is dependent on findings of fact made by the trial judge “that are demonstrably incompatible . . . with evidence that is neither contradicted by other evidence nor rejected by the judge” (para. 98); in other words, in cases where on examination the substratum of findings on which the verdict rests disappears.
holdings.statement: An appellate court may find a verdict unreasonable if it depends on findings of fact by the trial judge that are demonstrably incompatible with evidence that is neither contradicted nor rejected by the judge.

holdings.quote: However, it is useful to recall that in Sheppard we observed more broadly that: . . . the requirement of reasons is tied to their purpose and the purpose varies with the context. At the trial level, the reasons justify and explain the result. The losing party knows why he or she has lost. . . . Interested members of the public can satisfy themselves that justice has been done, or not, as the case may be. [para. 24] As a practical matter, these functional concerns are equally applicable to an appellate court’s consideration of an appeal based on the allegations of unreasonable verdict or a verdict that cannot be supported by the evidence.
holdings.statement: The requirement of reasons is tied to their purpose, which varies with context; at trial, reasons justify and explain the result, and this applies equally to appellate review of unreasonable verdicts.

holdings.quote: For that reason, I concur with Charron J. in the dismissal of the appeal.
holdings.statement: The appeal should be dismissed because the key issue is credibility and the trial judge's reasons do not justify reversal.

holdings.quote: 82 In this case, Alain Beaudry, an experienced municipal police officer with an impeccable record, stands convicted of obstruction of justice for having failed to perform his duties upon the arrest of Patrick Plourde, a member of the Quebec police force (the “Sûreté du Québec”).
holdings.statement: Alain Beaudry, an experienced municipal police officer with an impeccable record, was convicted of obstruction of justice for failing to perform duties upon arrest of a Quebec police officer.

holdings.quote: The uncontradicted evidence is that Mr. Plourde was in an advanced state of intoxication when arrested at the wheel of his car. He was taken to the station, but was not asked to provide the breath or blood sample necessary to determine the concentration of alcohol in his blood.
holdings.statement: The arrested Quebec police officer was intoxicated and was not asked to provide breath or blood samples to determine alcohol concentration.

holdings.quote: 84 I would therefore allow the appeal and set aside Mr. Beaudry’s conviction. In the circumstances, however, I would order a new trial and not substitute an acquittal.
holdings.statement: The appeal should be allowed and Beaudry's conviction set aside, but a new trial should be ordered rather than an acquittal.

holdings.quote: 88 The majority in Gagnon did not address this issue and I find it necessary and appropriate to revisit it here before proceeding to apply what I believe to be the appropriate test.
holdings.statement: It is necessary and appropriate to revisit the issue of the appellate court's duty under s. 686(1)(a)(i) before applying the appropriate test.

holdings.quote: 89 Section 686(1) (a)(i) empowers a court of appeal to allow the appeal “where it is of the opinion that . . . the verdict should be set aside on the ground that it is unreasonable or cannot be supported by the evidence”. In my view, the disjunctive “or” indicates a clear Parliamentary intention to differentiate between verdicts that cannot be supported by the evidence and verdicts that may properly be characterized as unreasonable on some other ground.
holdings.statement: Section 686(1)(a)(i) empowers an appellate court to set aside a verdict if it is unreasonable or cannot be supported by the evidence, with the disjunctive 'or' indicating a distinction between these grounds.

holdings.quote: To construe the test otherwise would be to permit for appeals, including appeals as of right, a narrower scope of curial review than for intervention by way of prerogative writ — where no appeal lies, with or without leave.
holdings.statement: A narrower scope of curial review for appeals than for prerogative writs would be inconsistent with the statutory language of s. 686(1)(a)(i).

holdings.quote: 90 It is important to remember that the unreasonable verdict test has more often than not been described and explained in cases involving jury trials, where particular considerations govern: See, for example, R. v. Yebes, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 168.
holdings.statement: The unreasonable verdict test has often been described in cases involving jury trials, where special considerations apply.

holdings.quote: 91 Unlike judges, juries are neither required nor even permitted to give reasons. Their reasons, in this country at least, are forever shrouded in the compelled secrecy of their deliberations: Section 649 of the Criminal Code prohibits the disclosure, subject only to narrow exceptions, of any information relating to the proceedings of a jury. Why the jury concluded as it did is thus beyond the ken of the court, both at trial and on appeal.
holdings.statement: Juries are neither required nor permitted to give reasons, and their deliberations are secret under s. 649 of the Criminal Code, so the reasons for their verdicts are unknown to the court.

holdings.quote: 92 Appellate courts are no more entitled to speculate about than to know how or why the jury reached its verdict. The jury is presumed to have been composed of reasonable people acting reasonably. It follows that its verdict must be deemed to be reasonable unless no properly instructed jury could reasonably have reached that verdict or, in the words of s. 686(1) (a)(i), it “cannot be supported by the evidence”.
holdings.statement: Appellate courts cannot speculate about how or why a jury reached its verdict, and the verdict must be deemed reasonable unless no properly instructed jury could reasonably have reached it or it cannot be supported by the evidence under s. 686(1)(a)(i).

holdings.quote: 93 The same, however, cannot be said for the verdict of a judge. The delivery of reasoned decisions is inherent in the judge’s role: R. v. Sheppard, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 869, 2002 SCC 26. And evaluating the reasonableness of those reasons is not a matter of speculation. Moreover, while the necessary degree of detail will vary according to the circumstances of the case, the reasons must be sufficient to permit meaningful review on appeal.
holdings.statement: The same presumption of reasonableness does not apply to verdicts of judges, who must deliver reasoned decisions that allow meaningful appellate review.

holdings.quote: 98 I hasten to add that appellate courts, in determining whether a trial judge’s verdict is unreasonable, cannot substitute their own view of the facts for that of the judge or intervene on the ground that the judge’s reasons ought to have been more fully or more clearly expressed.
holdings.statement: Appellate courts cannot substitute their own view of the facts or intervene because the trial judge's reasons should have been more fully or clearly expressed.

holdings.quote: But where reasons do exist, a verdict cannot be reasonable within the meaning of s. 686(1) (a)(i) if it is made to rest on findings of fact that are demonstrably incompatible, as in this case, with evidence that is neither contradicted by other evidence nor rejected by the judge.
holdings.statement: A verdict cannot be reasonable if it rests on findings of fact demonstrably incompatible with uncontradicted and unrejected evidence.

holdings.quote: Mr. Plourde had crying fits throughout the action, so we put him, for his protection, in the room for minors so that he would be better . . . .
holdings.statement: Mr. Plourde had crying fits throughout the action and was placed in the room for minors for his protection.

holdings.quote: 110 In short, the appellant’s conduct in this affair has been marked by transparency and not concealment throughout.
holdings.statement: The appellant's conduct has been marked by transparency and not concealment throughout the incident.

holdings.quote: In his contemporaneous and signed report, he stated that Mr. Plourde was apprehended in an [translation] “advanced state of intoxication”. He again disclosed this fact in his activity log, which was available for inspection by his superiors.
holdings.statement: The appellant stated in his contemporaneous and signed report that Mr. Plourde was apprehended in an advanced state of intoxication and disclosed this in his activity log available to superiors.

holdings.quote: And when the appellant brought Mr. Plourde to the police station, he placed him in a cell under video surveillance rendering it virtually impossible for anyone to deny that Mr. Plourde was intoxicated.
holdings.statement: When the appellant brought Mr. Plourde to the police station, he placed him in a cell under video surveillance making it virtually impossible to deny Mr. Plourde was intoxicated.

holdings.quote: Finally, lest any of this might otherwise have gone unnoticed, the appellant left a note for his superior officer suggesting that Mr. Plourde’s superiors be informed of the incident.
holdings.statement: The appellant left a note for his superior officer suggesting that Mr. Plourde's superiors be informed of the incident.

holdings.quote: 111 None of this evidence is disputed. None of it depends for its veracity on the credibility of any witness. None of it supports the inference that the appellant sought to conceal Mr. Plourde’s offence. None of it provides a reasonable foundation for the findings of fact upon which the trial judge caused his verdict to rest.
holdings.statement: None of the evidence is disputed, depends on witness credibility, supports concealment of Mr. Plourde's offence, or provides a reasonable foundation for the trial judge's findings.

holdings.quote: More particularly, none of it can reasonably be said to establish that the appellant failed to obtain breath samples from Mr. Plourde because he wished, for an improper motive, to hinder or foreclose the prosecution of Mr. Plourde. And that, as mentioned earlier (at para. 101), is the critical issue in this case.
holdings.statement: None of the evidence can reasonably establish that the appellant failed to obtain breath samples from Mr. Plourde due to an improper motive to hinder prosecution, which is the critical issue.

holdings.quote: 112 With respect, I therefore feel bound to conclude that the trial judge’s decision is unreasonable within the meaning of s. 686(1) (a)(i) of the Criminal Code .
holdings.statement: The trial judge's decision is unreasonable within the meaning of s. 686(1)(a)(i) of the Criminal Code.

holdings.quote: Accordingly, I would allow the appeal and order a new trial.
holdings.statement: The appeal is allowed and a new trial is ordered.

holdings.quote: 113 The integrity of our legal system depends in large measure on the integrity of those charged with its administration and enforcement. This assumes, so far as criminal justice is concerned, that police officers will act without fear or favour in the apprehension and prosecution of offenders.
holdings.statement: The integrity of the legal system depends on the integrity of those charged with its administration and enforcement, assuming police officers act without fear or favour in apprehension and prosecution.

holdings.quote: It is therefore essential, and not just understandable, for concerns to arise whenever there are grounds to suspect a police “cover-up” to protect one of their own or to please someone to whom they might feel otherwise beholden.
holdings.statement: It is essential for concerns to arise when there are grounds to suspect a police 'cover-up' to protect one of their own or to please someone to whom they might feel beholden.

holdings.quote: 114 Neither bad judgment nor an inappropriate — or even suspect — exercise of discretion by police officers in the execution of their duties are in themselves conclusive evidence of an attempt to obstruct justice.
holdings.statement: Neither bad judgment nor an inappropriate or suspect exercise of discretion by police officers in their duties is conclusive evidence of an attempt to obstruct justice.

holdings.quote: We must be no less zealous in avoiding injustice to police officers than in scrutinizing their dubious failures to investigate offences or to prosecute offenders.
holdings.statement: We must avoid injustice to police officers as zealously as we scrutinize their failures to investigate offences or prosecute offenders.

holdings.quote: 115 In this case, there was evidence upon which a trier of fact could reasonably find the appellant guilty as charged. But the appellant was nonetheless entitled to a decision that was supported by the reasons upon which it was said to be founded.
holdings.statement: There was evidence on which a trier of fact could reasonably find the appellant guilty as charged, but the appellant was entitled to a decision supported by the reasons upon which it was founded.

holdings.quote: 116 For the reasons given by Chamberland J.A. in the Court of Appeal, and for those set out above, I am satisfied that the verdict cannot stand.
holdings.statement: The verdict cannot stand for the reasons given by Chamberland J.A. in the Court of Appeal and those set out above.

holdings.quote: In my respectful view, however, a new trial would be more appropriate than an acquittal since the record contains evidence that, properly weighed and considered, could reasonably have supported a conviction.
holdings.statement: A new trial would be more appropriate than an acquittal since the record contains evidence that could reasonably have supported a conviction if properly weighed and considered.

rebuttals.quote: However, this aspect of his analysis has no impact on the question before us: whether the verdict was unreasonable.
rebuttals.court_answer: The limitation of police discretion by extrinsic factors has no impact on the question of whether the verdict was unreasonable.

rebuttals.quote: If so, there is no need to go any further, since, as I have already mentioned, police discretion is an essential component of our criminal justice system.
rebuttals.court_answer: If the conduct is a proper exercise of police discretion, there is no need to go further because police discretion is an essential component of the criminal justice system.

rebuttals.quote: It would therefore be paradoxical to say that conduct that tends to defeat the course of justice can at the same time be justified as an exercise of police discretion.
rebuttals.court_answer: It would be paradoxical to say that conduct that tends to defeat the course of justice can at the same time be justified as an exercise of police discretion.

rebuttals.quote: It is, however, equally applicable to the judgment of a judge sitting at trial without a jury. The review for unreasonableness on appeal is different, however, and somewhat easier when the judgment under attack is that of a single judge, at least when reasons for judgment of some substance are provided. In those cases, the reviewing appellate court may be able to identify a flaw in the evaluation of the evidence, or in the analysis, that will serve to explain the unreasonable conclusion reached, and justify the reversal.
rebuttals.court_answer: The Yebes test is equally applicable to judgments by trial judges without juries, though review for unreasonableness is somewhat easier when reasons are provided.

rebuttals.quote: I do not agree that the trial judge made such errors. Moreover, it is important to note that that is not the issue before this Court. This is an appeal as of right concerning the question of law whether the verdict is unreasonable within the meaning of s. 686(1) (a)(i).
rebuttals.court_answer: The trial judge did not make such serious errors, and the issue before the Court is whether the verdict is unreasonable under s. 686(1)(a)(i), not whether errors in interpretation occurred.

rebuttals.quote: There would be no need for this requirement if the sole test of unreasonableness under s. 686(1) (a)(i) is whether there is any evidence capable of supporting the verdict.
rebuttals.court_answer: If the sole test of unreasonableness under s. 686(1)(a)(i) were whether any evidence supports the verdict, there would be no need for judges to provide reasons.

rebuttals.quote: No one should stand convicted on the strength of manifestly bad reasons — reasons that are illogical on their face, or contrary to the evidence — on the ground that another judge (who never did and never will try the case) could but might not necessarily have reached the same conclusion for other reasons.
rebuttals.court_answer: No one should be convicted based on manifestly bad reasons just because another judge might have reached the same conclusion for other reasons.

rebuttals.quote: A verdict that was reached illogically or irrationally is hardly made reasonable by the fact that another judge could reasonably have convicted or acquitted the accused.
rebuttals.court_answer: A verdict reached illogically or irrationally is not made reasonable by the fact that another judge could reasonably have convicted or acquitted.

rebuttals.quote: 105 With respect, the appellant’s explicit disclosure in these documents that Mr. Plourde was in an advanced state of intoxication could only have attracted attention to — not diverted attention from — that very fact. The judge’s inference in this regard is plainly contradicted by the very evidence from which it was drawn.
rebuttals.court_answer: The appellant's explicit disclosure that Mr. Plourde was intoxicated in these documents could only have attracted attention to that fact, contradicting the judge's inference that they diverted attention.

rebuttals.quote: 106 Similarly, the trial judge’s characterization of the “depression excuse” as a subsequently concocted justification is inconsistent with the undisputed evidence.
rebuttals.court_answer: The trial judge's characterization of the 'depression excuse' as a subsequently concocted justification is inconsistent with the undisputed evidence.

rebuttals.quote: 107 Moreover, the distinction between the words “depressed” and “mentally disturbed” is more semantic than significant. And the absence of the word “depressed” in the police report is also of limited importance.
rebuttals.court_answer: The distinction between the words 'depressed' and 'mentally disturbed' is more semantic than significant, and the absence of the word 'depressed' in the police report is of limited importance.

rebuttals.quote: Rather than undermining the appellant’s assertion, this evidence aptly demonstrates the tenuous foundation of the Crown’s case.
rebuttals.court_answer: The absence of the word 'depressed' in the police report does not undermine the appellant's assertion and demonstrates the tenuous foundation of the Crown's case.

rebuttals.quote: I refuse to believe that the guilt or innocence of an accused can depend on whether or not a given word appears in a report. The purpose of the document is to report on an incident and the ensuing police action; it is not not a medical report, even though the words used describe what some would naturally associate with a depressive state: . . .
rebuttals.court_answer: The guilt or innocence of an accused cannot depend on whether or not a given word appears in a report, which is meant to report on an incident and police action, not to serve as a medical report.

rebuttals.quote: 108 Finally, the trial judge’s reliance on Marc Rocheleau’s testimony is inconclusive at best.
rebuttals.court_answer: The trial judge's reliance on Marc Rocheleau's testimony is inconclusive at best.

rebuttals.quote: 109 Assuming this evidence to be true, as indeed we must, the only inference to which it reasonably gives rise is as consistent with innocence as with guilt. Mr. Rocheleau’s evidence is of little assistance in that regard, either on its own or in the context of the evidence as a whole.
rebuttals.court_answer: Assuming Rocheleau's evidence is true, it only reasonably supports an inference consistent with innocence as with guilt and is of little assistance in determining the appellant's motivation.

authorities.quote: What La Forest J. said in R. v. Beare, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 387, at p. 410, is directly on point here: Discretion is an essential feature of the criminal justice system. A system that attempted to eliminate discretion would be unworkably complex and rigid.
authorities.authority: R. v. Beare, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 387, at p. 410, supports that discretion is an essential feature of the criminal justice system and eliminating it would make the system unworkably complex and rigid.

authorities.quote: Thus, the police practices manual cannot transform the discretion to decide whether or not samples should be taken into a binding legal rule: Maple Lodge Farms Ltd. v. Government of Canada, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 2.
authorities.authority: Maple Lodge Farms Ltd. v. Government of Canada is cited to support that administrative directives cannot transform police discretion into binding legal rules.

authorities.quote: 46 In R. v. Jageshur (2002), 169 C.C.C. (3d) 225, the Ontario Court of Appeal addressed this question in a context that was very similar to the one now before us. That case concerned the legality of a police operation carried out in compliance with the applicable law but not with the applicable administrative directives. Doherty J.A. wrote the following for a unanimous court: An officer’s duties and hence his or her responsibilities cannot be equated with instructions as to how those duties and responsibilities should be carried out. Police policies speak to the manner in which police should carry out their responsibilities, but do not define or limit those responsibilities. . . . My conclusion that the officers’ responsibilities were not circumscribed by the RCMP policy concerning major drug operations and reverse stings is fortified by a consideration of the nature of these policies. Section 21(1) (b) of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act authorizes the Governor in Council to make regulations for the conduct and performance of duties by members of the RCMP. Section 21(2) (b) authorizes the Commissioner of the RCMP to make rules (standing orders) for the conduct and performance of duties by members of the RCMP. Section 38 of the same Act authorizes the Governor in Council to make regulations governing the conduct of members (Code of Conduct). The policies in issue on this appeal did not spring from any of these statutory sources. . . . [Emphasis added; paras. 50 and 52.] In short, evidence of the existence of directives of this nature and evidence that the accused was, or is presumed to have been, aware of them at the time of the conduct in issue can shed light on the circumstances of the alleged exercise of his discretion. The same is true of evidence about the police service’s usual procedures, such as the testimony of Assistant Director Rocheleau and retired officer Lapointe in the case at bar. However, such evidence cannot be conclusive. 4.1.2.2 The distribution of responsibilities between Crown prosecutors and the police does not eliminate police discretion
authorities.authority: R. v. Jageshur clarifies that police policies guide how duties are carried out but do not define or limit police responsibilities.

authorities.quote: The comments of Iacobucci and Major JJ. for the majority of the Court in Housen v. Nikolaisen, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235, 2002 SCC 33, are worth repeating: While the theory has acceptance, consistency in its application is missing. The foundation of the principle is as sound today as 100 years ago. It is premised on the notion that finality is an important aim of litigation. There is no suggestion that appellate court judges are somehow smarter and thus capable of reaching a better result. Their role is not to write better judgments but to review the reasons in light of the arguments of the parties and the relevant evidence, and then to uphold the decision unless a palpable error leading to a wrong result has been made by the trial judge.
authorities.authority: The comments of Iacobucci and Major JJ. in Housen v. Nikolaisen emphasize the importance of respecting the trial judge's privileged position and the finality of litigation in appellate review.

authorities.quote: 79 In R. v. Sheppard, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 869, 2002 SCC 26, we held that a trial judge’s failure to deliver reasons sufficient to permit meaningful appellate review was an “error of law” within the scope of s. 686(1)(a)(ii).
authorities.authority: In R. v. Sheppard, a trial judge's failure to deliver sufficient reasons for meaningful appellate review was an error of law under s. 686(1)(a)(ii).

authorities.quote: 87 In R. v. Gagnon, [2006] 1 S.C.R. 621, 2006 SCC 17, Justice Deschamps and I, dissenting in the result, held that “[t]he duty of an appellate court is not limited to ensuring that ‘the verdict was available on the record’” (para. 36). This is because s. 686(1) (a)(i) of the Criminal Code specifically provides that a verdict may be set aside on appeal if it is “unreasonable or cannot be supported by the evidence”.
authorities.authority: In R. v. Gagnon, the duty of an appellate court is not limited to ensuring that the verdict was available on the record, because s. 686(1)(a)(i) allows setting aside a verdict if it is unreasonable or unsupported by evidence.

authorities.quote: 94 This fundamental distinction between jury verdicts and verdicts rendered by trial judges was explicitly recognized in R. v. Biniaris, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 381, 2000 SCC 15, where Arbour J., speaking for the Court, explained the matter this way: The review for unreasonableness on appeal is different, however, and somewhat easier when the judgment under attack is that of a single judge, at least when reasons for judgment of some substance are provided. In those cases, the reviewing appellate court may be able to identify a flaw in the evaluation of the evidence, or in the analysis, that will serve to explain the unreasonable conclusion reached, and justify the reversal.
authorities.authority: R. v. Biniaris recognizes the fundamental distinction between jury verdicts and judge verdicts, explaining that appellate review for unreasonableness is easier when a single judge provides reasons, allowing identification of flaws justifying reversal.

authorities.quote: 95 See also R. v. Burns, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 656, particularly at p. 665, and R. v. Burke, [1996] 1 S.C.R. 474.
authorities.authority: See also R. v. Burns and R. v. Burke for related principles on appellate review of verdicts.

authorities.quote: That is beyond the purview of an appellate court: R. v. W. (R.), [1992] 2 S.C.R. 122; Burke; Biniaris; H.L. v. Canada (Attorney General), [2005] 1 S.C.R. 401, 2005 SCC 25; R. v. Kerr (2004), 48 M.V.R. (4th) 201, 2004 MBCA 30.
authorities.authority: The limitation on appellate courts substituting their view is supported by R. v. W. (R.), Burke, Biniaris, H.L. v. Canada, and R. v. Kerr.

authorities.quote: As Chamberland J.A. stated: [translation] The fact that the word “depression” does not appear in the incident report is not, in my opinion, determinative, or at any rate it is not sufficient to support a finding that the appellant’s explanations are unreliable or do not, at the very least, raise a reasonable doubt.
authorities.authority: Chamberland J.A. stated that the absence of the word 'depression' in the incident report is not sufficient to support a finding that the appellant's explanations are unreliable or do not raise a reasonable doubt.

left_open.quote: This issue cannot be settled properly without first discussing police discretion generally and, more specifically, its relationship to the offence of obstructing justice.
left_open.issue: The issue of unreasonableness cannot be properly settled without first discussing police discretion generally and its relationship to the offence of obstructing justice.
left_open.reason: Needs discussion of police discretion and legal principles first

left_open.quote: Once the applicable legal principles have been established, it will be possible to consider how the trial judge applied them to the evidence.
left_open.issue: Once the applicable legal principles have been established, it will be possible to consider how the trial judge applied them to the evidence.
left_open.reason: Application of principles to evidence to be considered later
